en: May Sarasvatī herself, whose body is worshipped as being fashioned from the Vedas and Shastras, grant you every boon— she, by relying upon whose grace the words of even the teachers of the world flow forth with manifold virtues unimpeded.
Having struck down the torment of obstacles, may my work’s seed grow through the falling rains of my favor.

Entreated by me, may Gaṇeśa— the cloud that is exceedingly white— sprinkle and cause to sprout the fruit of my desires, which is never in vain. I bow to those gurus, by the mass of whose dust, which dispels the mire of darkness, my own soul has attained clarity.
Just as that very reality (tattva) is perceived through verbal testimony as a means of valid cognition,
so do we compose this work for the purification of our own intellect.

Since the determination of the capacity [of a means of knowledge] regarding its specific object depends upon the comprehension of the nature of verbal testimony as a means of valid cognition, [the author] restates its definition, well-known in the world, in order to define the nature of verbal testimony as a means of valid cognition.
The wise declare that verbal cognition (*śābda*) is that certain knowledge which arises from the cognition of a word regarding an object not present to the senses.
This is the summary: verbal cognition is the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) consisting of the cognition of an object not in contact [with the senses] arising from the cognition of a word.

He shows the alternative views that are to be excluded by the qualifiers applied to those possessing the characteristic of height: "The speaker’s intention, the means of knowledge, [the status of] the object, and even the mark (liṅga); cognition, another means of knowledge, and desire—these are excluded by the qualifiers. (6)

On this point, some say: words bring about the comprehension of the speaker’s intention (*vivakṣā*) or another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding the meaning of the sentence, but not the mere object itself.
And it is those two, as comprehended through the word, that serve as the cause for linguistic usage regarding the object.
This was stated by Dharmakīrti: "They indicate what is intended by the speaker."
He replies to them: "The cognition is with respect to the object.

Even though it is held that there are only two means of valid cognition—perception and inference—the comprehension of an object does not arise from verbal testimony alone; rather, it arises from a mark (liṅga) that is invariably concomitant with the object.
As it has been said:
"Perception and inference are the two means of valid cognition,
because that which is not perceived is understood through a connection with something similar."

Thus [it is argued]: verbal cognition is inference because it brings about understanding by way of a universal, because it is a means of valid knowledge other than perception, because its object is the three worlds, and because it depends on the knowledge of a relationship, just like the cognition of fire from smoke.
To refute that, he says: "From the cognition of the word... (śabdavijñānāt).

As for the objection that— since the definition of scripture (*āgama*) is "the instruction of a reliable person" (*āptopadeśa*)— words convey their objects by depending upon other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), he replies to that with the word "not in contact" (*asannikṛṣṭa*).
Now he states the manner of refutation regarding the first [position]:
"Intention is not cognized through the activity, which is focused solely on the object;
rather, it perceives only the fact that [the activity] was the cause of the utterance, even subsequently. (7)
In this regard, the comprehension of the speaker’s intention (*vivakṣā*) does not first arise from words.

For a child, by means of the sign of activity (*pravṛtti*) directed toward an object—which occurs immediately after the cognition of the word—infers that the cognition [of the listener] has as its object a specific thing, on the grounds that it is the effect of the word; it does not infer that the cognition has as its object the speaker’s intention and so forth, because there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for apprehending that.

[Objection: But surely, when a person who is proficient [in language] uses a word himself, having personally experienced his own state of intention and so forth, he understands through inference that the previous cognizer also possessed that same state.

Likewise, the preceding cognizer also understands at that very moment, through inference based on his own self, the state of the desire to speak (*vivakṣā*) and so forth residing in the speaker who employs [the word]. Having subsequently ascertained the capacity of the word within that cognition, he understands in his own self that the desire to speak and the like are the cause for the employment of that [word], and not that they are the object of the word, because he has no knowledge of the word's capacity to denote them there. He understands this in the same way regarding the two previous agents—the speaker and the cognizer—and thus does not postulate the capacity of the word therein.
Furthermore, the desire to speak and so forth are not the sole meaning of the word, because linguistic usage occurs with respect to the [external] object.
Furthermore, if [the cognition] were to project an object due to some logical necessity (*anupapatti*), it might take on just any object whatsoever.
If, however, it is excluded from non-objects (*arthavyāvṛtta*), then the object itself is its domain, because of the absence of deviation (*avyabhicāra*).

Moreover, in the case of conceptual cognition (*savikalpaka*), since it is attached to specific verbal expressions regarding the mere object, the speaker's intention (*vivakṣā*) and so forth are established otherwise as being merely inferable.
Because there is no word that denotes it, and because it would lead to an over-extension (atiprasaṅga) for something that is not the meaning of a word to be the meaning of a sentence;
therefore, as far as the knowledge of capacity is concerned, the object itself is the domain of the word.
Now, he refutes the position of inference (anumāna):

The essential nature (svabhāva) and the effect (kārya) would not exist [as valid reasons], nor would there be any restriction of place and so forth. Furthermore, because of the connection with capacity, inference would not be observed as having the property of being a predicate of the subject (pakṣadharmatā). There are only three types of logical marks (liṅga) possessing the three characteristics: essential nature, effect, and non-perception (anupalabdhi).

In this regard, first of all, the relation between word and object cannot be non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*), because it is of a positive nature (*bhāvarūpa*). Nor can exclusion (*apoha*) be the word-meaning, because as long as "cowness" is not apprehended, the exclusion of "non-cow" cannot be established, and because such a conceptualization is untenable.

Furthermore, there is no essential connection (*svabhāvānubandha*) between them—such as that which exists between "treeness" and "śiṃśapā-ness"—due to the absence of identity (*tādātmya*) through inherence in a single substrate (*ekārthasamavāya*).
Nor can there be a co-inherence in a single object based on the speaker's intention and so forth, because a single locus is not perceived.
Nor is there a causal relationship between them, as in the case of smoke and fire, due to a lack of evidence.
Furthermore, sound does not arise solely from the mere intention to speak.

If it is argued that the word "cow" (*go-śabda*) originates from the speaker’s intention (*vivakṣā*), [we ask: how can there be a verbal expression (*abhilāpa*) of the object of that intention by means of the word "cow," given that the object is not apprehended by it? [This objection is rejected] because we accept that the object, being non-substantial (*avastu*), lacks causal efficiency (*ahetutva*). Furthermore, since verbal expression is associated with conceptual cognition (*savikalpaka*) to that extent, and since the knowledge of the relationship [between word and object] occurs in that very [conceptual cognition], the word possesses a relationship of denotation (*bodhakatva*) toward the object—even though the word is produced by the intention to speak and so forth.
Nor is there a restriction of place between these two [intention and word], such as [the relation] where there is cool shade, there is coldness.
Nor is there a restriction of time, such as that when the rising of Kṛttikā occurs within a two-ghaṭikā period, Rohiṇī will follow.
This is because [the relationship] lacks fixed spatial and temporal conditions.
Therefore, since there is no invariable concomitance (avinābhāva) between these two, sound is not an inferential mark (liṅga) for the object.
From what connection, then, does the comprehension of an object arise from a word?
From that which is characterized by the capacity for the cognition thereof.
[Objection: In the absence of a connection with the object, how can there be such a capacity for its cognition?
We do not say that there is a connection by way of the object itself, but rather by way of the cognition thereof;
and that connection is held to be characterized by the capacity for producing that [cognition].
But if there is no other connection, how can there be the capacity for producing that cognition, as fire has in producing smoke?
For in that case, there is no other concomitant [cause] by virtue of that capacity.

Now, if it is argued that in that instance fire alone is the cause and there is no such thing as "capacity," yet smoke still arises from the fire, then let cognitions of objects likewise arise from words.
Or, if it is argued that in the production of cognition there is a dependence on another concomitant, but not in the production of every effect whatsoever; [then we reply:]...
For no "concomitant" (anubandha) is observed in the case of the eye that is distinct from the capacity for the cognition of the object.
Now, if it is argued that the cognition of the apprehended object is caused by another concomitant— which is not seen due to the [non-perception of] the word and its meaning—
then there would be an inference based solely on a concomitant characterized as a "capacity" (śakti).
For it is well known that inference consists in cognition based on a capacity [of a mark] that is qualified by a specific relation.
[Objection: But surely, inference is cognition arising from a perceived relation.
[Reply: True.

Because it has grasped the relationship through the object, cognition is distinct from the mere capacity of that [object's] cognition; however, cognition is not inference solely by virtue of its connection to the capacity of that cognition.
Now, one might ask: "In this much, how is there a distinction from other means of valid cognition (pramāṇa)?
Or what constitutes the full extent of this distinction from other means of valid cognition?"

Moreover, the subject (dharmin), the property (dharma), the presence of the property in the subject (pakṣadharmatā), and the example (dṛṣṭānta) are not required for the cognition of meaning through words.
For this reason as well, there is a distinction between [verbal] inference.
But surely, precisely because of this lack of a causal complex for cognition, words would lack authority (aprāmāṇya).
It is not [inference], because, unlike the cognition of fire from smoke, we observe that words do not fail to correspond with their objects when conveying meaning.
And thus is the formal argument:
verbal testimony is not inference, because, while being independent of any other relation to be cognized, it possesses the capacity to produce a cognition of the object, just like the eye.
Therefore, perception is the cause of comprehension by its own power through the fact of being unknown [to the senses].
Inference is the cognition arising from that which has been grasped as possessing the three characteristics (trairūpya).

Verbal testimony is the cognition regarding that [object] arising from a word grasped as having the capacity to produce such a cognition; thus, it constitutes a distinct means of valid cognition (pramāṇa).

Therefore, it is correct [to say] "from the cognition of the word. Now, he states the method of refutation regarding the position that [the Veda] depends on other means of knowledge: "It is not accepted that the word depends on other means of knowledge, whether in the Veda or in common worldly usage."
For the cognition of the speaker serves indeed to remove defects that may have been incurred by the word;
however, in the case of the Veda, we shall explain its independence from other means of knowledge through the demonstration of its non-human origin.
But in the case of what is of human origin, one must discern: "Of what use would the cognition of the speaker be?"

If it is held that [the speaker’s cognition] produces either the cognition of the word or the cognition of the object, or the valid cognition (*pramiti*) thereof, in that case, the speaker’s cognition does not produce those two while remaining unapprehended; for even by way of the listener’s intellect, there is no connection [between them], since both the agent and the instrument require a connection for the production of an action.

If, on the other hand, it is apprehended, how could the speaker’s cognition—which is excluded from what is unapprehended and unvalidated—be understood with respect to an object that is itself unapprehended and unvalidated?
Furthermore, a cognition that is apprehended without an object can never be a cause of valid cognition.
Is it not the case that word-meanings are understood from words?
True;
however, the speaker’s knowledge is not required for that much alone.

In that case, let the relation also be apprehended through general observation or through creative imagination; for once this [relation] is indeed apprehended, there is no longer any talk of the capacity of words—whether as words themselves or as word-meanings already understood—to bring about the comprehension of a relation that is distinct from the words.

Even when words and other factors are present, if there is no comprehension of the speaker’s specific cognition, there is an absence of certainty regarding the relation [between word-meanings]; and conversely, even in the absence of words and other factors, if that [cognition] is present, we do not observe an absence of certainty regarding the relation. Since certainty regarding it is established from that [cognition] alone, words and the rest—being otherwise established as causes of the cause—are not proven to be auxiliary causes for the relation.
In that case, how could this apply to the Veda, which lacks the speaker’s cognition and depends on a power established by worldly usage?
Therefore, since the sentence-meaning is indistinguishable [from the worldly case], the establishment of the relation must proceed from the words themselves.
Is it not the case that at the time of grasping the word’s expressive power (*śakti*), the power is understood as residing in the relation?
True; however, at the time of comprehension, that [power] is not required, because the determination of the relation arises from the speaker’s cognition alone.

Alternatively, even in that case, at the time of comprehension, the apprehension of the power in the relation should be considered an error, according to the very same logic observed [in other instances].

Therefore, it must be admitted that the determination of the relation [between word-meanings] arises from the words themselves, in accordance with the apprehension of their semantic capacity (*sāmarthya*). In this regard, when there is a contradiction with other means of valid cognition (*mānāntara*), and because the word-meanings have not been previously associated in actual usage, the fault lies in the fact that the words denoting those meanings are brought together in the intellect by being connected with case-endings (*vibhakti*) suitable for mutual syntactic connection (*itaretarānvaya*). From that fault inherent in the words, erroneous cognition (*bhrāntijñāna*) arises. Furthermore, it is understood through positive and negative concomitance (*anvayavyatireka*) that this fault residing in the words is produced either by an erroneous cognition or by a conceptual construction (*utprekṣājñāna*) regarding the object on the part of the speaker, mediated by the act of utterance.
In that regard, the authority of the speaker is useful by way of eliminating such defects, but not as a cause for valid cognition (*pramiti*).
When there is a connection with a person, the scripture must necessarily depend upon him because defects may be suspected;

however, in the case of the Veda, there is no suspicion of defect, because it arises from the cognition produced by the application [of words] which is caused by another cognition directed toward its meaning—the cognition resulting from the proximity of words joined with case-endings capable of mutual syntactic connection.
Nor does it depend on the exclusion of that [error]; thus it is said to be independent (*nairapekṣya*). Otherwise, as has been stated, there would be no attainment of valid cognition in the Veda.
Therefore, in this way, even in the world, there is no dependence for the production of valid cognition.
[Objection: But surely, memory—which is produced by another cognition having the same object—is dependent; likewise, it should be so here as well.
That is not so;

for in that case, there is dependence because the object is mixed with that of another means of knowledge (māna), whereas in inference—such as the cognition of pervasion produced by the knowledge "fire is the pervader"—it would be the same [if it were otherwise].
But here, there is no such mixing.
"Because the word has its capacity for the mere object.
Therefore, the inclusion of the term "not proximate" (asaṃnikṛṣṭa) is appropriate. Thus, it is established that the definition of verbal cognition is indeed correct.
But what, then, is denoted by the word "word," from which cognition of an object arises through a cognition of its form?
He says: it is the universal (*jāti*).
Even the word "word" [denotes] that universal, because it is indivisible and because it is not perceived [as a distinct entity].
Recognition occurs even prior to the advent of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) and prior to conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), just as it does in common worldly experience.
(Kārikā 10) When a single denotative term is observed to apply to distinct objects, it must depend either upon a difference in its expressive power (*śakti*) or upon a universal (*sāmānya*).

If there were a difference in expressive power, there would be an infinite number of things to be denoted, resulting in an incapacity to know the relationship [between word and meaning] and the fault of excessive conceptual complexity (*kalpanā-gaurava*).
It might be argued: "Just as the word 'cook' (pācaka) does not depend on those two [the specific object and the universal], so it would be here as well.
This is not tenable.

For in that case, because the word is etymological (yaugika), its application—even in the absence of those two—is possible across various distinct objects through its connection with the general sense of the meanings of its constituent parts.
Furthermore, this indivisible word does not denote specific instances of sound through the power of its parts; rather, it must have the universal alone as its objective referent. [Objection:

But words such as “this is its cause” and so forth denote specific instances by relying on an adventitious attribute (*upādhi*). Likewise here, let the word "sound" (*śabda*) also denote specific instances by relying on the adventitious attribute of being perceivable by the auditory organ. [Reply: That is not so, because it is impossible to have a reflective awareness of a denotation based on an attribute when that attribute has not been previously apprehended.

For when a previously unperceived specific word-sound (*śabda-viśeṣa*) is now being perceived, there can be no reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) of it as such, because the auditory organ, the cognition thereof, and the fact of its being grasped by that organ are not themselves objects of direct perception (*adhyakṣa*).
Furthermore, in the initial cognition, the designation [of the object] is superimposed upon it.

[Objection: But surely, once that sound is characterized by the property of being graspable by the auditory organ—as inferred from the cognition of the object—there could be a reflective awareness of its designation.

It is not possible to infer that [an object] is graspable by the ear without an understanding associated with a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) regarding its name and its object, which has a form similar to what was previously apprehended;
for the mere awareness of being experienced is not the cause for the understanding that something is graspable by that [sense].
Indeed, at that very moment, it is impossible to determine graspability through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), because the other sense organs are also present.

Nor can its status as an object of perception be inferred merely by its difference from what is grasped by other sense organs, because it also possesses a difference from other objects grasped by those same organs.
Furthermore, a universal is established only when there is similarity (*sālakṣaṇya*).
Nor is there even a unity of the limiting conditions (*upādhi*), since the ears and so forth are distinct; for a universal is impossible in the case of things that are eternally inferable.

Therefore, even when perceiving a word that has not been heard before, one must accept a universal (*sāmānya*) as being apprehended by the first cognition; this is for the sake of connecting it with its denotation, avoiding a multiplicity of potencies, and understanding its status as something perceivable by the auditory organ.
Now, it might be argued that a universal derives its existence from recognition (*pratyabhijñā*), and thus cannot find a place in the absence of such recognition.
To this we reply: the reflective judgment "this is that" (*so 'yam*)—which constitutes recognition—is indeed present even in the case of a well-known universal.

If there were indeed a continuous connection with the mere form within the cognition [of the word], then for one who has perceived a sound, there would be an apprehension of a form distinct from the object in another sound, by which means there would first be an association with the denotation—as has been stated.

Furthermore, another sound is not perceived as being identical in substance, taste, and so forth [to the first]. Moreover, the postulation of identity regarding the external denotable object is based on the postulation of identity regarding the auditory organ and other limiting adjuncts.

Let it not be [objected] that because [qualities] such as acute (*udātta*) and grave (*anudātta*), or sharpness and softness, are perceivable by the sense of hearing, they would constitute the meaning of the word "sound" (*śabda*); for [in that case], there would be grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between the word "acute sound" and so forth, and the substratum (*dharmin*) which is itself the word.
Therefore, the postulation of a universal (*jāti*) alone is superior.
Consequently, it is established that verbal cognition (*śābdī buddhiḥ*) is a cognition of an object as qualified by that universal.

Now, he examines the word as the cause for the comprehension of meaning: "Does the cognition of meaning arise from a word distinct from the phonemes, or from those [phonemes] refined by the impressions of their own cognitions, or from remembrancers distinct [from them], or from the phonemes themselves? (11)

Some maintain that the cognition of the meaning of a word arises from that which is designated as a "word" (pada), which is distinct from the individual phonemes and serves as the objective basis for the single unitary cognition of the word.
Others hold that it arises through the mental impressions (saṃskāras) produced by the cognitions of the phonemes, which serve as the causes for the recollection of those phonemes.
Still others assert that the cognition of the meaning arises from those very same impressions, once they have transcended their status as mere causes for recollection.
Some maintain that [the cognition arises] from the phonemes alone;
he accepts the latter position as his own:
"The phonemes, acting together with the impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by their respective cognitions which cause recollection..."
"Gradually, through a single recollection, the Buddhas perceive the meaning directly.
(12) In order to establish this by means of refuting the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*), he describes the theory that the word is distinct from the phonemes (*varṇa*):
"Cognition [of the word] is not obtained from each individual phoneme, even though it exists..."
Cognition does not arise from the aggregate [of phonemes], whether that aggregate is unperceived, perceived, or remembered;
for an aggregate is impossible, and because the causes are distinct.
Therefore, it is understood that this cognition arises from the word itself, as something distinct from the individual phonemes.
There is, indeed, the cognition of an object immediately following the perception of phonemes such as *ga* and so forth.
It must be investigated whether this [cognition] arises from the phonemes themselves or from a word distinct from them.
First of all, it does not arise from each individual phoneme, whether perceived or unperceived, because such a result is never observed.
Nor can it arise from the collection of phonemes (*varṇa*), because such a collection does not exist.
For this very reason, the cognition of meaning does not result from the perception or the recollection of a collection of phonemes.

Furthermore, since the causes of perception—the utterances of the phonemes—occur sequentially and are distinct, and since the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) which cause recollection are likewise distinct as they serve as independent causes for the recollection of each individual phoneme, neither the simultaneous perception nor the simultaneous recollection of all the phonemes is possible.

Therefore, since the understanding of meaning is derived from something other than that which is determined by perception—namely, the single word "this" which is postulated through inference based on the residual evidence of meaning and cognition—it follows that the comprehension of meaning arises from a word distinct [from the individual phonemes].
Now, he refutes this position:
"That which exceeds the phonemes is not perceived; the phonemes, when accompanied by their adjuncts, constitute the word."
When the meaning is not understood, there is no single word; nor is there a connection [of the word] even when another sound occurs.
(15) First of all, a word—which would either be inherent in the phonemes or independent like a jar—is not apprehended by perception as something distinct from the phonemes.
[Objection: But surely this word is perceived as a single entity distinct from the separate phonemes.
First of all, it is because it is impossible for the auditory faculty to perceive three phonemes, such as *ga* and so forth, simultaneously.
Nor is there a cognition of sound that is devoid of the perception of phonemes.
Furthermore, a word is not manifested by the phoneme *ga* alone, because this would apply equally to words such as *gaṅgā*.
Truth is indeed manifested therein, but it is specifically determined by the subsequent phonemes.
Even so, without the recollection of the three phonemes, the word that conveys the specific meaning is not manifested.
And that recollection cannot be based on the sense organ of hearing, because it is impossible.
Nor is a word manifested as something distinct from the phonemes—like "cowness" (gotva) is manifested in individual cows such as Khaṇḍa—in the mere letter *ga* alone.
Nor can the word be an object of mental perception (*mānasapratyakṣa*), because the three phonemes are not apprehended simultaneously.

If it is argued that the word is superimposed upon the mind when the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by the cognition of each individual phoneme have reached their full maturity through the cognition of the final phoneme—this is not so; for the word does not appear without the coloring (*anuparāga*) of the three phonemes, and a simultaneous coloring by them is logically impossible.

Now, if the mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by the perception of each individual phoneme were to combine and produce a single recollective cognition (*smṛti-jñāna*) having all the phonemes as its object,

then the word-cognition (*pada-vijñāna*) which takes those recollected phonemes as its support would not be a direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), just like the whiteness perceived in a recollected jar. Furthermore, since the understanding of the meaning (*artha-buddhi*) is established from such a recollective cognition alone, the postulation of a "word" (*pada*) is purposeless.
"Surely the word (pada) appears [as a distinct entity].

True; it is the phonemes themselves that, under the limiting condition (upādhi) of their capacity to convey a single meaning, come to be designated as a 'word'—just like a forest [is designated for its trees].
But surely, even prior to the ascertainment of its expressive power (śakti), the word is apprehended."

When an unfamiliar language is being exemplified, an unlearned person lacks the knowledge of how to divide the words; consequently, due to uncertainty regarding whether there is one word or many, the usage of "words" by students even in the case of *saṃhitā* (continuous phonetic junctions) is based on a tradition of usage by those possessing such [erroneous] cognitions. Therefore, the cognition of a "word" is merely conditional (*aupādhikī*) and has as its object only the phonemes (*varṇa*).
But has it not been stated that there is no cognition of meaning from the phonemes?
True; however, the aforementioned logical inconsistency applies equally even to the manifestation of a word as a means of cognition.
Now, suppose a single memory, resting upon three phonemes, manifests the word.
In that case, it would be the same even regarding the manifestation of meaning;
and it must be stated for the sake of conventional usage regarding the fixed number of phonemes that manifest the word,
for a number is not perceived without a reference to the things numbered.
Therefore, since there is no reason to postulate a word distinct from the phonemes, it is most reasonable that the comprehension of meaning arises from the phonemes alone.
He describes the second prima facie view:
"The latent impressions themselves, when fully awakened by recollections, are the remembrancers."

Having acquired the capacity through the cognition of the meaning, they directly cause the meaning to be understood. (16) It is precisely the impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by the perception of the phonemes that cause the meaning to be conveyed, serving as the cause for the recollection of those phonemes.
[Objection: But how can those [phonemes] which are not being perceived at the time [of conveying the meaning] function as conveyors, like the eye and other sense organs?

This is not a fault, for it is possible [for the cognition of meaning] to arise from those very impressions (saṃskāra) which have been reinforced by the recollection of the phonemes that constitute their own respective effects. [Objection: But the apprehension of a previously unknown object is never seen to result from impressions alone. [Reply: True; however, in this case, just as in the case of recognition, the apprehension of the object arises from those same impressions—assisted by the cognition of the final phoneme and accompanied by the present sensory contact—with the impression of the prior perception acting as the cause. This is understood precisely from the observation of the immediate effect.
It is said:
The cognition of the object would not arise from the recollection [of the letters], because it is not perceived elsewhere;
rather, that cognition arises precisely from the letters as established in their sequence, due to the similarity [of the sequence] with what is well-known. (17)
First of all, the impression (*saṃskāra*) produced by the cognition of one [letter] does not cause another object to be understood, because such a restriction is never observed.

If it is argued that [this capacity] is postulated on the basis of the efficacy of the result (*kāryasāmarthya*), then let the capacity of the letters themselves—precisely those perceived in succession—be postulated for that very reason.

But how can the efficacy of the cognitions of the preceding letters, which existed in the moments prior to the cognition of the final letter, be postulated as having a causal capacity when there is an interval of time, given that such a thing has never been seen before?
This assumption of an unseen capacity (*adṛṣṭasāmarthya*) in simultaneous impressions is equal [to the alternative].
What, then, is the reason for the definitive conclusion?

Because the impossibility [of the alternative] is equal and because the comprehension of meaning from words is well-established, the position that [the word] consists in the perception of the phonemes (*varṇa*) alone is superior.

Even in the case of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*), only the component consisting of memory arises from the mental impression (*saṃskāra*), and there is no apprehension of something previously unknown. Furthermore, even the cognition of the final phoneme [of a word] does not act as a cooperative cause.

For if it were maintained that the cognition of the relation [between words and meanings] arises from the words themselves, then at the time of the cognition of the final phoneme of the sentence, the cognitions of the final phonemes of the individual words would have ceased to exist.

Nor is it the case that the cognition of the final phoneme of a sentence alone, acting in conjunction with the entire word, [produces the meaning]; for if that [cognition] were included within the words as having specific, non-abiding phonemes, it would follow that the words themselves could not be determined. If, on the other hand, it is not included because the nature of the word differs in every usage, then the incapacity of a word—which is merely a mental impression (*saṃskāra*)—to convey even a portion of its own denoted object remains a settled fact. Furthermore, the view that "from words come word-meanings, and from those comes their relation" will be refuted later.
Moreover—
In the case of a change in order or a difference in the speaker,
there would be no comprehension of the relationship and so forth, because the mental impression (saṃskāra) remains the same and because the cognition of the complete impression is lost.
Even when phonemes are uttered in a reversed order, the cognition of the meaning would occur due to the lack of distinction in the impressions.
Why should it not be the same in the case of the phonemes (*varṇa*) as well? Because there is a fixed rule regarding their specific order.
If that is so, then that same rule would apply to the mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) as well.

However, a fixed rule for the order of their production is not employed for the comprehension of meaning; for once the production of the impressions has occurred immediately after the final phoneme, that production—and thus its order—has already passed away.
Nor is there a sequence of space and time [for the word], because it exists simultaneously in one place.
But surely, even for phonemes (*varṇa*), there is no sequence of space and time, owing to their all-pervasiveness and eternity.
However, the sequence of apprehension has already passed away immediately after the apprehension of the final phoneme.

There is no fault [in our position], because we admit that even though the sequence has passed away, it serves as a cause by being colored (*uparakta*) by the memory-cognition which apprehends all the phonemes without exception; furthermore, we do not accept the position that the sequence is the object of perception itself.

Moreover, such a memory must be explained; otherwise, there would be an impossibility of the linguistic usage of "phonemes" and "words" characterized by specific sequences and numbers, since the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by so many phonemes in such a sequence—which have become the objects of a single word-cognition—would not lead to the comprehension of a single meaning.
As it was stated by the authors of the *Vārttika* on the *Autpattika-sūtra*:
And when the final phoneme is cognized,
others declare that there is a recollection of all the preceding phonemes produced by the mental impressions (*saṃskāra*).
Thus, according to the established conclusion (*siddhānta*),
there would indeed be a cognition of meaning even when [the words] are employed in a reversed order.

Furthermore, in the case of the theory of mental impressions (*saṃskāra*), the cognition of meaning that arises when [words] spoken by different speakers are also being mentally synthesized as characterized by a specific sequence would have to be independent of that sequence.
In that case, one might argue that the cognition of the mental impression (*saṃskāra*) produced by the successive [sounds] is the cause for the comprehension of the meaning.
This is not so, because there is no means of apprehending such a [mental impression].

If it is argued that the very effects of the recollection of the phonemes (*varṇa*) serve as the means of apprehension—this is also not the case, because those [recollections] too occur successively; therefore, a single cognition whose object is all the phonemes as presented in their sequence is impossible.

Furthermore, on this view, it would be difficult to account for such linguistic practices as: "the cognition of the relation [between word and meaning] arises from the cognition of the related [term]," "the understanding of the meaning arises from the known word," and "in conceptual cognition, there is a recollection of the denotation. If it is argued that all this is accomplished simply by the occurrence of a recollective cognition that reflects upon all the phonemes in their sequential order, then, since the meaning is established from that alone, it would be impossible to postulate any causal efficacy (*sāmarthya*) in the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*).

Therefore, because it is impossible for latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) to possess a novel capacity, because it contradicts established consensus, because it would entail undesirable consequences in cases such as the transposition of syllables, and because it is impossible to know the relationship [between them], the position of latent impressions is not superior; rather, it is established that the position of the recollection of phonemes (*varṇasmṛti*) alone is correct.

To those, however, who postulate apūrva-impressions as the revealers of meaning, distinct from the impressions produced by memory, he says: "An assumption of something non-worldly is improper due to the complexity of the assumption regarding an impression; since the understanding of meaning arises from the word itself, the assumption in that regard is simpler. (19)

Indeed, even by you who deny that a word is something over and above its constituent phonemes, a cognition that reflects upon all the phonemes without exception must be admitted for the sake of the conventional usage of words.

At that time, since the meaning is established from that very cognition, there is no room for the postulation of a supernatural latent impression (*saṃskāra*). Furthermore, such a postulation would involve unnecessary complexity (*kalpanā-gaurava*): namely, the capacity of the cognitions of the phonemes to produce a new latent impression, the nature of those latent impressions themselves, and their capacity to produce the cognition of the meaning.
This fault does not apply to the view that [cognition] arises from the recollection of the phonemes (*varṇa*).
But surely, latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) do not invariably produce recollection; for if they did, the cognition of the meaning would necessarily arise immediately after the final phoneme.
This same fault applies equally to the view that [the cognition] arises from a novel latent impression (*apūrvasaṃskāra*).
The assumption that [the phonemes] necessarily produce [the cognition of word-meaning] because such an effect is observed is equally applicable to the view that the phonemes are remembered.
Therefore, it is established that the comprehension of the meaning of a word arises from the phonemes themselves as they are being remembered.

And thus, in the *Devatādhikaraṇa*, the Bhāṣya states: "In the linguistic usage of elders, these phonemes, being grasped in their sequential order and having their relationship to specific meanings already apprehended, appear in exactly the same form even in one's own usage; following the perception of each individual phoneme, they manifest within a cognition that reflects upon them as a whole, and thereby cause their respective meanings to be understood without error.
Now, he examines the word (*śabda*) which is the cause for the comprehension of the sentence-meaning:
"From a sentence whose relationship with its constituent words has been grasped, [the meaning is understood] from that which possesses the parts of the words..."
Some maintain that the cognition of a specific relation arises from words or word-meanings themselves;

others maintain that the cognition of a specific relation arises from the sentence itself—which is distinct from the words and consists of indivisible units—once the relationship between words and their meanings has been grasped;
while still others maintain that it arises from the word-meanings as they are understood through the words.
Others have maintained that the cognition of the relation [of meaning] arises from the words themselves, which are capable of denoting the meanings in a combined state;
among these, he accepts the latter position as his own:
"By the words themselves, which possess the power to convey their own meanings as already related."
The relation, consisting of the nature of the subordinate and the principal, is being established.

To establish this by means of refuting alternative positions, he first refutes the position that it is the sentence [itself]: "Because of the absence of a means of knowledge for that, because of ignorance, because of infinity, and likewise because of the connection..."

Because of the infinity of capacities and the diversity of usages, a sentence cannot be the communicator [of meaning]. (22) First of all, a sentence—whether as something distinct from words, inherent in the words, or independent like a jar—is not capable of being perceived through direct perception by either the auditory organ or the mind. This is because the cognition of a single sentence is based on the limiting condition (upādhi) of a specific capacity for a single meaning, just as in the case of individual words; for this is not understood in the same way when a language is unfamiliar.

Furthermore, even if this [position] were accepted, since the sentence differs in every individual performance (*pratiprayoga*) through the insertion (*āvāpa*) and deletion (*uddhāra*) of words, it would possess a power distinct from the powers of the individual words; thus, it would be impossible to grasp its relationship with its denotable meaning (*śakya*).

If it is argued that this is not so because [the meaning is understood] from the knowledge of the relationship between word and word-meaning—how could one thing cause another to understand its meaning through the knowledge of a different relationship?

If, on the other hand, it is claimed that words are not entirely different from the sentence, but rather that the sentence itself is designated as "words" through a division based on external adjuncts (*upādhi*).

This is not sound. Even for an indivisible word such as "cow" (*gauh*), if there were a difference in its denotative power (*śakti*), one would require the knowledge of separate relations; how much more so when there is a difference in the possessors of that power? Now, if it is argued that in the former case the requirement arises because of a difference in the objects denoted (*abhidheya*), whereas here, since the sentence-meaning consists merely of the word-meanings joined together, there is no need to grasp a separate power for the sentence; [we reply: [This argument fails,] for even in the case of a single word like "cow," if its power were divided, the cognition of distinct relations would be required. How much more so when there is a division of the powers themselves? Furthermore, if you claim that in the case of a complex word like "cook" (*pācaka*) the requirement for distinct relations exists because of the difference in the denoted objects, whereas in the case of a sentence, since the sentence-meaning is simply the word-meanings conjoined, there is no need to apprehend a separate power for the sentence—this is untenable. For even in the case of a single word such as "cow," if its expressive power were split, one would have to rely on the knowledge of separate relations; how much more so when the powers themselves are distinct? It is not the case that, due to the difference in the objects to be conveyed, the sentence requires a separate cognition of its own power (śakti)—as is the case with the word "relation" (saṃsarga)—such that the apprehension of such a power would be untenable. Nor does a sentence convey meaning when its relationship [to its parts] is unapprehended, because it is a linguistic unit (śabda) like a word.

Furthermore, if one were to postulate a power of the sentence distinct from the powers of the words and their meanings, there would be the fault of conceptual complexity (kalpanā-gaurava), as the sentence would differ with every particular usage.

Likewise, in the case of the eight usages—"O child, bring the cow; O child, tie up the cow; O boy, bring the cow; O boy, tie up the cow; O youth, bring the cow; O youth, tie up the cow; O infant, bring the cow; O infant, tie up the cow"—eight distinct sentences and their respective potencies must be postulated. For those who maintain that the sentence is the primary unit (padavādins), however, there would be only seven. Furthermore, when another word such as "white" (*śuklām*) is employed, because the sentences become distinct, another set of eight sentences and their potencies must again be postulated.
But for those who maintain that [meaning resides] in words (*padavādin*), there is only one power; therefore, the position of the sentence (*vākya*) is futile.
Now, he sets forth the position of word-meanings (*padārtha*): "Since words cease their operation only after having conveyed the word-meanings..."
"Only the word-meanings themselves directly convey the relation subsequently.

The proponent has asserted that "abhihitānvaya" (the connection of what is expressed) consists in the word-meanings, once they have been understood from the words, conveying their own mutual relations. He states the proof for this:
Because the meaning obtained through insertion and exclusion (āvāpa-uddhāra) necessitates a specific substratum,
and because there is a sequence of cognition even from words despite their being separated [by others],
the connection [of meaning] is established; yet, since those two [sequence and connection] are otherwise established even from the meanings themselves, [the word is not the primary cause].
The capacity of words is determined to reside in their own forms alone.

In various applications such as "Bring the cow," "Tie up the cow," "Bring the horse," and "Tie up the horse," because the form of the cow is introduced when the word *go* is introduced, and it is withdrawn when that word is withdrawn, the denotation of the word *go* consists of that much alone; it does not consist of another object or its relation [to other things], because those would be subject to deviation (*vyabhicāra*).
Likewise, at the time of comprehension, from words such as "cow" and so forth, there arise only cognitions of the object itself in succession, not cognitions of another object or its relation.
The cognition of relation, however, follows after the cognition of the final word-meaning.

Thus, when it is understood through usage and cognition that the capacity of a word resides solely in the form of the object-meaning, then—by means of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) that cannot be otherwise accounted for—it is postulated that the word-meanings themselves are the causes of the cognition of relation which occurs immediately after the use of the sentence.

[Objection: But surely, by means of the sign of purposeful activity (*pravṛtti-liṅga*), it is precisely the cognition of relation that is understood through positive and negative concomitance as being the effect of the word.
That is not so, because those two [the meanings of the words] are established otherwise by virtue of being the objects of the causes of the causes.
Therefore, it is settled that the power of words resides in the mere individual forms (svarūpa) and not in the relation (saṃsarga).
To refute this, he proposes the theory of the expression of the related (anvitābhidhāna):

The wise declare that what is called the denotation of words is precisely their conveying of their own meanings as mutually related; this is the denotation of the related (anvita-abhidhāna). Regarding this, he states the proof: [Verse 26]... [He states the proof therein—]

For, by means of the activity of the person who acts, it is inferred without any intervening step that the learner has acquired a cognition of the relation [between word and object], which is itself bound to the cognition of the words.
Indeed, once the cognition of the relation has been inferred from the activity, the positive and negative concomitances (anvaya-vyatireka) reveal the causal capacity of the word.
Now, it may be argued that [the relation] is established otherwise through the intervention of the cognition of the word-meanings.

This is not so; for at that time there is no apprehension of such an intervention, nor can it be established at a later time by following that [intervention], because the process of insertion and deletion (avāpoddhāra) is possible precisely by means of that [direct apprehension].

Nor is there a rule in the world that the apprehension of a qualified object must be produced by the apprehension of its qualifiers, since when the eyes and other sense organs of the perceiver are the same, the apprehension of the qualified object occurs right from the very beginning.
Therefore, it is established that from the very beginning, positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka) indicate the capacity for syntactic relation (saṃsarga-sāmarthya).
Now, one might object: "Even so, it has been stated that through insertion and deletion (āvāpa-uddhāra), the capacity resides in the word-form alone.
To this, he replies:

Because one observes the insertion and deletion of a word's own meaning as it is conjoined with what is compatible or otherwise, the capacity of words is determined to reside only in their being combined [with others].

(28) Although, in every specific usage, deviation is seen regarding other particulars and their respective relations, nevertheless, because there is no deviation in its own meaning being conjoined with what is compatible, the capacity is postulated to reside in that very [conjunction] in accordance with the capacity for relation understood first; such is the intended meaning.

Nor is it logical that the insertion and deletion of the relation [occur] through the insertion and deletion of the knowledge of word-meanings; for since that [knowledge] exists prior to the relation, it is impossible for there to be positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka) with the relation at that time, as its priority at that time—unlike that of the word—is not established.

Now, it might be argued that "cowness" (*gotva*) as merely related to another object is not the domain of the word "cow's" (*gośabda*) potency, because this would entail the consequence that the connection with "bringing" (*ānayana*) is non-verbal.

Furthermore, since the mere relation to another object is established otherwise through inference and so forth even when the word denotes only its own form (*svarūpa*), it is not logical to postulate the word’s potency for that purpose.

If, on the other hand, one were to postulate that "cowness" as specifically related to "bringing" is the denotation of the word "cow," then the consequence would be the uselessness of the other word "bringing."
To this he replies: "We do not speak of a connection with a universal, but rather of a connection with a particular;
even regarding the object, the injunction is equal, and the expectation is a cooperative factor. (29)

For even one who maintains that it is the word-meanings themselves—such as "cowness" and so forth—that cognize their mutual internal connection by virtue of expectancy, proximity, and compatibility, must admit that those word-meanings do not convey a connection with another word-meaning in its mere generality; this is because both linguistic usage and cognition are established as being restricted to specific connections, and because a general relation would otherwise be redundant.

Now, if a word conveys its own meaning as already associated with a particular other object-meaning, then the employment of further words would not be purposeful for the sake of understanding those other meanings, since the specific relation [of the first meaning] would be established by that single meaning alone. If, on the other hand, it is argued that even though the word-meanings are capable of conveying the relation, they do not convey it without depending upon one another—just as even potent causes require auxiliary factors (*sahakārin*) to produce an effect—then this same logic applies equally to words. For even those words, which are capable of conveying the relation, convey it only through mutual dependence.

For this very reason, even though the word "cow" possesses the capacity to convey its connection with every specific object—whether fit or unfit—it does not fail to function as the cause of a particular effect in a specific place and at a specific time, depending on the presence of auxiliary causes; this is no different from the case of the referent (the object) itself.

Now, one might object: when the word "cow," which is capable of denoting connections with all specific objects—both fit and unfit—is employed, how can the specific [object] required by it be supplied by the verb "bring" (*ānaya*), given that "bring" too is capable of connecting with many particulars and thus lacks any restriction to a single one?

It might be argued: "Only the word uttered first functions in the denotation of the related meaning (*anvitābhidhāna*), while those uttered last function by denoting their own forms (*svarūpa*) and thereby restrict that meaning.

This is not so; because there is no fixed rule regarding which word is uttered first in the employment of words, one must admit that all words possess the capacity for *anvitābhidhāna*, and thus the proposed restriction is unestablished. Alternatively, it might be argued: "The verb (*ākhyātapada*) alone denotes the related meaning, while the other words denote their own forms and thereby restrict that meaning."
That is not so, because there is a lack of evidence, and because it is impossible to deny the observation of the syntactic connection between word-meanings even in sentences devoid of verbal forms.
Therefore, the restriction regarding their mutual relation is not established even through mutual dependence; to this, he says:
"Since there is no dependence upon mere form, the restriction is not contradicted."
Because the objection applies equally even to the [other] meaning, the two [terms] are not synonyms.

(30) Even though words such as *go* possess the capacity to denote a relation (*saṃsarga*), they possess the capacity for cognition regarding the mere essence of "cowness" (*gotva*) and so forth without depending on auxiliary factors when each word is used individually, since this is observed to be the case.

Indeed, it is impossible to restrict that in all instances—even regarding what is possible—there must be either dependence on auxiliary factors or independence from them; for in the world, both are observed, as there is dependence in some cases, such as moving, reading, or eating, and independence in others.

Therefore, since words collectively cognize word-meanings—which are themselves the objects of cognitions produced by words independent of one another—as being mutually related, there is no contingency of indetermination.

Furthermore, even regarding a single word-meaning, which is capable of producing a cognition of its connection with all its qualifiers, by what specific distinction would one restrict the connection [to a particular qualifier] when other auxiliary word-meanings are also capable of producing cognitions of multiple connections?

Now, if it be argued that because [the word] is more highly esteemed, it must restrict [the relation] by its own form alone, then the word also, having restricted the relation through the form of the word-meaning—which is the object of an independent cognition—would cognize it; thus, there is no contradiction whatsoever.
For this very reason, it is specifically stated that "cowness" and so forth are the primary meanings of words such as "cow," because they are the objects of independent cognitions.

It might be objected: in the usage "Bring the cow," since the two words denote their respective meanings as mutually related, there would be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of their being synonyms.

This is not sound. For if the same meaning that is understood from one word—when independent of other words acting as its auxiliaries—were also understood from another word taken alone, then those two words would indeed be synonyms; however, such is not the case here, because their status as having a single effect is caused solely by their mutual dependence. Therefore, there is neither the uselessness of the other word nor any lack of restriction. It might be argued: "Since the relation varies with each specific usage due to the difference in the related relata, and since the relation is capable of being differentiated, it would follow that an infinite number of powers must be postulated for a single word, such as 'cow'."
Regarding this, he says:

"Because the diversity of effects is established through diverse cooperation, the capacity (śakti) does not differ among objects, nor likewise among words, just as in the case of the sense organs. (31)
Indeed, even an object, while conveying a relation, would have its power differentiated according to the specific distinction of that relation due to the difference in the relations themselves.

Now, if it is argued that the diversity of effects is established by a single power through the variety of auxiliary factors (*sahakāri*), just as the eye—despite having only a single power to illuminate form—produces a diversity of effects in the form of cognitions of blue, yellow, and so on, solely due to the difference in auxiliary objects such as blue or yellow;
then, in the case of words as well, a diversity of effects resulting from a difference in auxiliary factors cannot be denied.

But surely, because there is an infinity of differences in the objects to be denoted for every particular instance, it would be impossible to grasp the relationship [between word and meaning]. And if that were possible, the word would merely be a restatement (anuvādaka). On the other hand, in the view that the object is the primary factor, there is no dependence on knowing the relationship, because this [grasping of the relationship] is a property of the word. To this, he says:

Because their connection is established through the application of secondary indication (upalakṣaṇa), like that between smoke and fire, there can be no acquisition of meaning (vyutpatti) from this; thus, in the case of such associations, they are merely restatements (anuvāda).

For just as there is a pervasion of the class of smoke by the class of fire, and by means of this indicative mark (*upalakṣaṇa*) the connection of the particulars is also grasped, so too, from the observation of a particular instance of smoke in specific locations, a corresponding particular instance of fire is inferred; yet this cognition is not a mere restatement (*anuvāda*). In the same way, although the capacity [of a word] for its own meaning is understood through the inclusion of the indicative mark—namely, that it is conjoined with particulars characterized by being either capable or otherwise—the capacity for the entire range of relations is nonetheless apprehended.
It is untenable that the cognition of a qualified relation arises from the utterance of a qualified [word], nor is that cognition a mere restatement (*anuvāda*).

For while in inference one cognizes only the general nature of fire, in verbal cognition as well, the relation is indeed restated; even when [the object] is merely indicated (*upalakṣaṇa*), the mere nature [of the object] necessarily requires dependence on another means of knowledge for its establishment.
Therefore, it is established that the relation is not a restatement.
This might be the case: if the universal *gotva* (cowness), when conjoined with a meaning not already expressed by another word, were denoted by the word "cow," then other words would be redundant.

On the other hand, if it were denoted by what has already been expressed, there would be the fallacy of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatā*): once "bringing" (*ānayana*) is expressed, the word "cow" would denote *gotva* as conjoined with it; and once *gotva* is expressed, the verbal root "to bring" (*ānayat-i*) would denote the act of bringing as conjoined with it. To this, he replies: "The meanings understood in succession, and then simultaneously combined..."
"Let them measure the word-meanings"—thus there is no fault of mutual dependence (anyonyāśraya).
For the word-meanings are understood sequentially from the words independently of one another;
and immediately after the utterance of the final word, those very same words convey those same word-meanings as being mutually related. Thus, there is no fault.
Alternatively, it is not the prior comprehension of the meanings of words as unrelated entities that is required here; rather, such comprehension is merely incidental.
Therefore, it is established that words, being grasped simultaneously, convey the relation [of meaning], and thus the connection (anvaya) occurs precisely through the act of denotation itself.

Consequently, at the time of actual usage, it is established by positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka) that the capacity of words is not determined to reside in their mere individual forms alone, but rather in the relation [they express].

As for the claim that only the mere meaning of the word is apprehended from each individual word and not the relation, and therefore the capacity (sāmarthya) resides in that alone—that too is incorrect. For it is possible for that which is capable of [producing] the relation to serve as a cause for the cognition of the mere essential nature (svarūpa) when lacking its auxiliary factors; otherwise, there would be the cumbersome assumption of multiple powers (śakti)—namely, the power of words toward their word-meanings and the power of word-meanings toward their mutual relation.

It might be argued: "Even in the view that the word is the primary factor, the capacity must reside in one's own meaning as qualified by other word-meanings; thus, it follows that the capacity itself possesses qualifiers."
That is not so; for even the power of the word's meaning possesses a qualification, insofar as its object is its own nature as excluded from other things.
Therefore, let it be accepted that the cognition of the relation [between words and meanings] arises from the words themselves by way of restating the essential natures of the word-meanings.

Regarding this, someone says: "The cognition of a word-meaning from a word is not a restatement produced by the capacity of denotation; rather, since the knowledge of a word-meaning from a word must be one of the following—recollection, valid cognition, doubt, or error—it is, by process of elimination, simply recollection."
And that [recollection], being caused by the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) of a previous perception, does not depend upon verbal expression.

Furthermore, the cognition of a word, having as its object a word connected with a meaning, serves as the cause for the recollection of another related thing by means of awakening the latent impression.
What, then, is this relation between a word and its referent?
It is characterized precisely by the capacity for that cognition.
If that is so, then let cognition be accepted as arising from that very capacity; what is the point of postulating a further capacity for memory in relation to that which possesses the power?
This argument is not sound.

"Because it is impossible for that which is capable [of denoting] a qualified object to have its power [to denote] reside in the mere essential nature [of that object], and because a cognition of only that much [the mere nature] would be untenable.
To this, he says:
"If it is incapable with respect to the mere essential nature, how could it be a recollector of that?"
If [it is argued that] the cognition arises from a connection with only a portion of the capacity, then let the capacity itself be the cognizer.
The meaning is this: just as there is a recollection of a single part from a word connected to a qualified object, so too the function of denotation is possible in that much alone.
Furthermore—
Cognition [of one related object] does not arise from the word by way of necessity, because it occurs through the observation of something possessing a common connection;
nor would there be any power [in the word] regarding objects, since the recollection of them occurs even when there is a relation [between the word and the object].

(35) First of all, the cognition of one related object from the sight of another related object is not necessary, because such relations are manifold and because it is impossible for there to be a fixed recollection of a specific speaker or other factors in any single instance.

Furthermore, for one who possesses the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) resulting from the apprehension of the relationship [between word and meaning], the cognition of the object necessarily arises upon the perception of the word. Moreover, if [the cognition] were produced by a latent impression, then the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) with the word would be disregarded.

Nor can it be argued that the word is established as something else (i.e., not the cause of cognition) merely by its being an awakener of the latent impression that causes remembrance; for no awakening of a latent impression distinct from remembrance itself can be defined, and because it would follow that [the word] would awaken latent impressions regarding the speaker and other such objects.

Therefore, since the denotative function (*abhidhāna*) itself—qualified by the impressions (*saṃskāra*) resulting from the knowledge of the relationship—is the complete cause for the cognitions of word-meanings, this [cognition] necessarily arises as a restatement (*anuvāda*).
Furthermore, because it lacks the blending (*saṃbheda*) of previous perceptions along with their place, time, and so forth, it is not memory (*smṛti*).

Moreover, since the impressions of the individual word-meanings persist even at the time of the cognition of the relational synthesis (*saṃsarga*), it would follow that they result in mere memory; thus, the function of denotation could never be established in respect to them.
Furthermore, because the relationship with the expressive power (śakti) is unknown, the recollection of one related object does not arise from the perception of another related object.

Indeed, it cannot be maintained that at the time of the cognition of the connection, the cognition of the word-meanings produced by the denotative function (abhidhāna) did not already exist, even though the latent impressions (saṃskāra) are present.
Therefore, this is a restatement (anuvāda) produced by the denotative function.

It is established that this very [cognition] first arises from each individual word, and subsequently, through those very words acting as mutual auxiliaries, the relation (*saṃsarga*) is understood, because this involves a parsimony in the postulation of capacities (*śakti*).

Furthermore, if the relation were not being cognized from word-meanings already determined by other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), how could one postulate that the cognition of the relation—which possesses positive and negative concomitance with the perception of the words—is caused by the word-meanings?
It might be argued: "The words manifest the operation of the word-meanings toward the relation, or their capacity for it, but they do not constitute another means of valid cognition."
And thus, there would be no cognition of the relation [between word-meanings].

Furthermore, since the cause of the relation is not observed in words prior to the knowledge of their connection, how could the subsequent cognition of the relation—arising after the comprehension of the meanings of the words in their sequence—be based on the word?
To this, he says:
There is no manifestation of the power of relation (saṃsarga-śakti) from the word itself, nor is there a manifestation of its operation;
for those two are not the denotable meanings, nor is the word the cause of them.
Furthermore, the word has no other operation directed toward the object of denotation by which the power of relation and its operation might be manifested upon the comprehension of the word-meanings.
Nor can those two [the sentence and its meaning] be understood from the individual words, because they are not directly denoted by them.
Furthermore, the cognition produced by the words cannot be the cause of the excellence (i.e., the synthesis) of the word-meanings, because a cognition does not cause a modification in its own object.

Nor can it be postulated that, in the case of words that convey a relation through dependence on the apprehension of the connection, there is a causal role for the understanding of the word-meanings as a secondary consequence; for this would involve the fault of postulating an unnecessary capacity (*śakti-kalpanā-gaurava*) and because such a capacity has never been observed elsewhere.

Nor is it correct to say that there is no excellence [in the cognition] regarding word-meanings once they have been understood through words, nor when they are understood through other means of knowledge;
therefore, the cognition of relation is based on words.
But [an objection may be raised]: nanu...
For one who perceives the white color-form, hears the sound of neighing, and hears the sound of the trampling of hooves, there arises the cognition: "A white horse is running."
Thus, it has been shown that the cognition of relation arises even from the individual word-meanings themselves.
Therefore, he says:
"But the understanding of relation is not dependent on the [individual] meanings alone, without another means of knowledge."
For the cognition "the white horse is running" arises from the inference by elimination (pariśeṣānumāna).

When there is a requirement for a substratum (dharmin) for the running—inferred from the sound of the trampling of hooves—and for the whiteness—which is directly perceived—since no other substance is possible, one infers that these reside in a horse inferred from the sound of neighing by means of elimination; thus one understands "the white horse is running," and not from mere individual word-meanings alone.
Furthermore:
There is no inclusion [of objects] within the means of valid cognition (pramāṇas), because objects are impossible [therein];
nor is there [inclusion] in verbal cognition, because that [invariable concomitance] is not its defining characteristic, since it consists of inseparable connection (avinābhāva) and so forth.
First of all, objects do not convey their mutual relation like the eyes and other senses, because they are not causes [of cognition] as long as they have not been cognized themselves.
Nor is it like inference, because of the absence of an inseparable relation (*avinābhāva*);
nor is it through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), since the meaning of words is established even without a syntactic connection;
and similarity and non-existence (*abhāva*) have restricted objects.
Nor can it be included within verbal cognition (*śābda*), because the definition of the latter is "cognition of an object arising from a word.
[Objection: But surely the comprehension of a relation (*saṃsarga*)—even if produced by word-meanings that have been cognized through words—is indeed verbal.
[Reply: No, because since there is no relation between the word-meanings and the relation itself, they cannot function as the means of cognition.
Is it not the case that a relationship characterized by the nature of locus and located (āśraya-āśrayin) exists?
No, because that alone is not the cause for cognition;
for even when a jar is apprehended through a word, its locus, taste, is not cognized in the absence of [other factors] such as invariable concomitance (avinābhāva).
But surely, it is the words themselves that convey the relation, though mediated by the cognition of the word-meanings.
As it has been said:
"In their employment for the sake of cognizing the sentence-meaning, [the cognition of the word-meanings] is an inseparable concomitant."
The presentation of categories is like the lighting of wood in a fire for the sake of cooking.

This is not the core point; for since the understanding of word-meanings culminates in the words themselves—just as the act of cooking culminates in the flames—the connection between word-meanings cannot be the cause [of the sentence meaning].
Alternatively, it might be argued that the words themselves, serving as the instruments for the cognition of word-meanings, convey the connection.

[Objection: Because words whose relations have been grasped possess positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka) only with respect to their own accessories (upakaraṇa), the cognition of relation [of word-meanings] does not fall within the scope of valid means of knowledge (pramāṇa). [Reply:

But how can there be the function of indication (lakṣaṇā) in the theory of the expression of the related (anvitābhidhāna), given that it does not convey its primary meaning as being connected with another meaning?
Nor is it the indicated meaning (lakṣyamāṇa), because there is no word that expresses it.
Therefore, in that case, the connection is based on the indicated meaning.
And in the case of ellipsis (adhyāhāra), the connection is based solely on the meaning being supplied, since there is no word that expresses it.
Regarding this, he says:
"And in the case of indication (lakṣaṇā), the cognition of the relation would arise from the word expressing that [related object];
and in the case of ellipsis (adhyāhāra), it arises from the word obtained through verbal presumption (śabdārthāpatti). (39)

The word "bed" (mañca), having set out to convey its own primary meaning as conjoined with the act of "crying out" (krośana), produces a cognition of a person by means of the cognition of its own meaning—due to the contradiction [with the actual presence of people]—insofar as it is conjoined with the act of crying out.

For the referent of the word "bed," when understood from the word as being conjoined with the act of crying out, is the cause of the cognition of a person who is conjoined with the act of crying out, and not the word-meaning alone.

Therefore, since a word that is engaged in conveying a thing related to the meaning denoted by the proximate word serves as the cause for the cognition of a desired object—whether through mediation or without mediation—that relation is based upon it; thus, there is no contradiction in accepting the theory of *anvitābhidhāna* (the expression of the related).

Even in the case of the indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of an individual, because the cognition of the universal invariably culminates in the individual, the very expression of the relation of that universal is the cause for the relation with the particular as well.

Furthermore, since those words that express meanings are stated without syntactic connection, and since those words that possess such connection are not directly denotative, their capacity to convey meaning is indistinguishable [from other means].

Moreover, in the case of ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*), the establishment of the theory of "expression of the related" (*anvitābhidhāna*) is achieved through the supplementation of words obtained via presumptive implication (*arthāpatti*)—which concerns a portion of the valid means of knowledge capable of providing a portion of the object of cognition. Otherwise, if the connection with the elliptical meaning were based solely on the sense, it would follow that it lacks scriptural authority (*anāgamikatva*).
Therefore, he concludes:
"Thus, the connection [of meanings] is cognized from these words through their respective powers.
In this manner, I have established the theory of linguistic acquisition according to the principles and to the best of my ability. (40)
It has been stated that, according to the theory of *anvitābhidhāna*, the cognition of the relation [between word meanings] arises from the words themselves, which consist of phonemes.
Furthermore:
verbal character could not otherwise exist without the recollection of a collection of words.
Even in the case of a Great Sentence (*mahāvākya*), that [cognition] is indeed either non-conceptual or otherwise.

For this reason as well, one must admit that only words consisting of phonemes (*varṇa*) convey the meaning of a sentence; otherwise, because it would lack the nature of verbal cognition (*śābdatva*), the consequence would follow that it lacks validity (*aprāmāṇya*).

As for those who hold that the impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by the perception of phonemes alone are the remembrancers, or that something distinct from them—designated by the term "word" (*pada*) by virtue of being delimited by the capacity for the cognition of word-meanings—conveys the relation (*saṃsarga*), even by them, according to their own view, the verbal nature of the relation is intended, yet it is thereby refuted.

For how can one who asserts that the cognition of a relation produced by the objects perceived through words is non-verbal (aśābda) yet maintain that the cognition of a relation produced by the mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) generated by the perception of those [same] objects is verbal?
