Indeed, a cognition produced by the impressions of a visual perception does not itself become visual, nor does it become a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), because it lacks the quality of having an object not already apprehended (*anadhigatārthaviṣayatā*). If you argue this, then in the other case as well, who can prevent the same status [of being non-verbal] from applying, given that it is likewise produced by mental impressions?

Regarding this, he says: "In the view that [the sentence] consists of phonemes (*varṇa*), it is impossible to produce in the case of a great sentence (*mahāvākya*) a recollective cognition (*smṛtijñāna*) that reflects upon all the words immediately following the cognition of the final word as the cause of the connection; therefore, the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) themselves, independent of such a cognition, are the causes of that [connection].
This is not sound.

In a great sentence, there is no verbal valid cognition (*śābdī pramiti*); rather, the connection of those [words] whose relations have been understood, by virtue of their relation to a single purpose, is based solely on the meaning (*artha*).
Verbal cognition occurs only where there is syntactic unity (*padaikavākyatā*) among the words;
and since the number of words in such cases is small, the impossibility of mental synthesis (*anusaṃdhāna*) does not arise.

Furthermore, because the cognition of the relation (*saṃsarga*) for the other [type of sentence] is conceptual (*savikalpaka*), one cannot deny the necessity of connecting all the words expressive of that [relation].

Furthermore, a sentence is recited again and again for the sake of accomplishing the comprehension of all its constituent words without exception. According to the theory of mental impressions (*saṃskāra*), since those impressions arise from a single occurrence, there would be no need for repeated recitation; however, in the world, it is established through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) that the arising of a memory which comprehends all the words perceived in their proper sequence depends upon an accumulation of impressions.
It is not possible [to understand] that "this is a single sentence" unless one takes into account all the words as a whole, since there is no word that lacks a syntactic connection (ananvayi).
Alternatively, the consideration of all the words as a whole must be postulated because the cognition of the mutual relation (saṃsarga) would otherwise be inexplicable.
Furthermore, in the apprehension of the relationship [between words], if there is no consideration of all the words as a whole, there can be no comprehension of the capacity for mutual relation.
Therefore, the comprehension of the relation arises precisely from the recollection of the entire collection of words.

As for the one who postulates that the reflection upon all word-meanings immediately following the understanding of the final word-meaning is the cause of the relation—even for him, since that reflection on word-meanings is conceptual (savikalpaka), it must involve a reflection upon all the words that express those meanings; what then is the use of postulating a separate recollection of both?
Consequently, it is established that the relation arises solely from the reflection upon the entire set of words.

The theory of the expression of the related (anvitābhidhāna) has been stated. Now, he considers a certain specific point regarding that very same theory: "Does [the word] express its own meaning as connected with an action, or as conjoined with another meaning?"
Now, this is being deliberated: "Does the word denote [its meaning]? (42).

In this regard, the proponent of the theory that [the word's function] consists in the connection with an action (kāryānvayavādin) describes his own position: "For the activity of the cognizer is indeed bound to the cognition of the word..."
Only the cognition of a purposeful connection (*kāryasaṃsargadhī*) is determined by the learner.
Having inferred a specific cognition of a purpose through the sign of the hearer’s activity, he ascertains the capacity of words with respect to those objects that are connected to that [cognition].
Now, one might object: "Is it not the case that the very same cause of activity which was understood by the child in his own self is likewise inferred for the hearer?"

If it is argued that the cause of activity is then the knowledge of what is beneficial, or the knowledge of the means to achieve it, or the command and so forth, or the gestures and so forth [of another], to this he says: "Activity does not arise from the means to the beneficial, nor likewise from what is desired, nor from intention, for us; because of deviation and because of non-sublation, the cognition of 'what-is-to-be-done' (kārya) resides in the results and so forth. (44) This means: activity does not proceed merely from the knowledge of the means to the beneficial, nor from the mere desire for what is pleasant, nor from the intention of another. Why? Because there is deviation—since one may know the means to the beneficial or have a desire for it, yet fail to act—and because the cognition of "what-is-to-be-done" is never sublated with respect to the results and other such factors. Therefore, the cognition of "what-is-to-be-done" is the specific cause of activity.
Once the result and its means have been determined, one does not act toward them in their past or other temporal forms.

Therefore, even things such as the beneficial (*hita*) are causes for engagement only when they are apprehended by the cognition of "what is to be done" (*kārya*), because they are devoid of the three times [in that state].

Since there is deviation in the case of the beneficial and so forth, whereas there is no deviation in the case of the cognition of "what is to be done," that cognition alone is the cause of engagement.
Is it not the case that an action is indeed an effect only if it is a means to what is desired?
As it has been said: "For the worldly understanding is that something is 'to be done' (kārya) only when it is a means to what is desired by the agent."

Alternatively, since the cognition that something ought to be done (kartavyatābuddhi) is dependent upon the knowledge of the means for achieving a desired end, that [desired end] alone is the cause of activity by way of the cognition that it is a task to be accomplished; therefore, the expressive power of the word is postulated to reside in that very thing. Thus he says:
"The task to be accomplished is not the state of being a means to what is desired, for that is traditionally held to be the object of volitional effort (kṛti).
That [state of being a means] alone, because it is not separated [from the desired end], is the motivator even when the [task] has already been accomplished. (45)
The distinction between the "task" (kārya) and the "means to a desired end" (iṣṭasādhana) is well-established.

Although the cognition of taskhood is dependent upon the cognition of being a means to a desired end, it is said to be the immediate cause of activity. For the cognition that something is a means to a beneficial end—which itself depends on positive and negative concomitance—is not the direct cause of activity; rather, it is the cognition of taskhood [that is].
Therefore, it is established that the effect alone is the cause of activity (*pravṛtti*).
Regarding this, some say: "In verbal usage, the verbal productive urge (*śābdabhāvanā*) is the cause of activity.
In that context, *bhāvanā* is merely the sense of "doing" (*karoti*), which has the manifestation of what was previously non-existent as its result.

In this context, the operation upon the object is the objective productive urge (*arthabhāvanā*), whereas the operation of the word itself—characterized by the generation of a cognition of its own denotation—is the verbal productive urge (*śabdabhāvanā*). This [verbal productive urge] has the word as its agent, the production of the cognition of the object as its end, the cognition of the word as its instrument, and the mental impression (*saṃskāra*) from the cognition of the relationship [between word and meaning] as its procedure; it is common to all words without distinction.
However, it differs in the case of words such as those ending in the optative suffix (*liṅ*).

For that [efficient force] is relied upon as being established in the activity of the person, which is characterized by the efficient force directed toward the object consisting of the production of gender and so forth; it has its own cognition as the instrument (karaṇa) and the knowledge of explanatory passages (arthavāda) such as praise and censure as the procedure (itikartavyatā).

How so? Because the meaning of the verbal suffix (ākhyāta) is explained by means of the verb "to do" (karoti)—as in "he cooks" (pacati) meaning "he does cooking"—the meaning of "doing" is the denotation of all verbal suffixes.

However, when the optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and so forth are employed with the intention of expressing an injunction (*vidhi*), because they involve an activity directed toward a conscious agent, their denotable meaning is the sense of "doing" (*karoti*) characterized as the objective efficient force (*arthabhāvanā*). This consists of human effort, which has the fulfillment of a human goal as its end, takes the meaning of the verbal root as its instrument (*karaṇa*), and has the *prayāja* offerings and other such rites as its procedure (*itikartavyatā*). In this context, the specific distinction is that while the operation of the word—the optative suffix and so forth—generates knowledge of the objective efficient force (*arthabhāvanā*) which is its own denoted meaning, it also brings that very objective efficient force into being. How so?

Since we observe that activity follows immediately after hearing words such as the optative suffix (*liṅ*), and since a word whose relationship [to its meaning] has not been grasped does not incite activity, it is understood that a word incites one by denoting some object that serves as the cause of activity.

In this regard, because postulating the denotation of another object would involve a complexity of assumptions (*kalpanā-gaurava*), it is established—by means of the method of elimination (*pariśeṣa*) and presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*)—that the word, having performed its own denotative function characterized by the production of knowledge of the denoted object, generates the "efficient force of the object" (*arthabhāvanā*) which constitutes activity, by way of that [denoted object].

Therefore, the verbal productive energy (*śabdabhāvanā*) culminates in the realization of the objective productive energy (*arthabhāvanā*), and not merely in the realization of the knowledge of that [objective energy].

The cognition whose object is the verbal productive energy—which is produced by the denotative function (*abhidhāna*)—attains the status of an instrument (*karaṇa*) with respect to the verbal productive energy by way of accomplishing the realization characterized as activity, because it is a cognition that impels to action.

Furthermore, the cognition of the explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) consisting of praise or censure, which have as their object the objective productive energy accompanied by its three factors, experiences the status of the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) with respect to the verbal productive energy, because it serves as a cause for activity through the means of generating interest (*prarocanā*).

Thus, it is established that verbal productive energy (śabdabhāvanā), accompanied by its three components, is the cause of activity in linguistic usage. This [position] he refutes: "In the illustrative example, verbal productive energy is not observed to be the cause of activity."
Even regarding a word-meaning established by worldly convention, there is no presumption (*arthāpatti*) [of a verbal bhāvanā], because that would involve unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*).
First of all, this verbal bhāvanā has not been experienced by the child as the cause of his own activity, such that it could be inferred as the meaning of the word for the listener as well.

Nor is the denotation of its own expressed object understood through the methods of elimination (*pariśeṣa*) or presumption; for it is otherwise established simply by inferring the worldly effect [of activity], and because it would be complex to postulate two denotable objects for a single word—the verbal bhāvanā and the [external] denoted object.

Furthermore, regarding the operation of denotation (*abhidhāna-vyāpāra*), which is to be understood through the knowledge of the denotable object (*abhidheya-jñāna-gamya*), one should not postulate a separate capacity for the word therein, because that knowledge is established otherwise.

Nor can two cognitions having two denotable objects arise simultaneously from a single word, as there is no syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*) between the verbal meaning (*śabdārtha-bhāvanā*) and the objective meaning (*arthabhāvanā*), as is the case with the agent-number and the objective-bhāvanā.
Nor can they arise sequentially, because a word lacks the capacity to operate after having ceased its function.
Therefore, since its own nature is untenable and because it does not incite activity, it is established that the effect alone is the cause of engagement.
To this, it is replied:
Through positive and negative concomitance in the stages of instruction and so forth...
Children learn [the meaning] when it is associated with something else, but not merely as that which is connected to an action (kāryānvita).

Furthermore, the comprehension of the relationship between a word and its meaning is not achieved solely through the inference based on the sign of activity (pravṛtti) arising immediately after hearing the word; rather, instruction is also a means.
For instance, mothers and others generally instruct children regarding the relationships between words and their meanings.

And they ascertain the specific relationship there through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), just as in the case of the causal application (*prayoga*) and the instrumental condition (*pratyaya*).

Now, one might argue that even instruction such as "this is a jar" or "this is a cloth" is rooted in causal application; and since the grasp of linguistic competency (*saṅgati*) occurs within causal application regarding what is connected to an action (*kāryānvita*), such instruction must also be directed toward an action.
This is not so.
Since even practical application (*prayoga*) can be rooted in instruction (*upadeśa*), there is no "firstness" [in either]; for it is logical that these two stand as mutual foundations.

Nor is it the case that practical application is restricted solely to the "thing-to-be-done" (*kārya*); for in instruction as well, such restriction is understood by the learner, because the "thing-to-be-done" is not perceived as the object of the word's expressive power (*śabda-sāmarthya*) in instruction—since in instruction, one perceives merely a relation with something else.

It is better to assume that what is merely perceived as related in practical application is the denotable meaning (*abhidheya*), rather than postulating a "thing-to-be-done" that is not being perceived in the instruction itself.

Now, it may be argued that in the case of instruction (*upadeśa*), the capacity of a word to produce cognition cannot be apprehended, because—as in the case of actual usage—there is no means of knowing the effect of such cognition.
How then do children understand the meaning from a word used immediately after instruction?

If it is argued that since the capacity of a word to produce cognition is apprehended in some instances of usage, here too the capacity for cognition is understood through that commonality (*sāmānya*)—even so, in cases of instruction, the capacity for cognition is established even without an [observable] effect.

And likewise, the relations between words and their meanings are generally explained as having as their objects desire, aversion, and so forth, which are the powers of passion (*rāga*); for it is impossible to show that these [powers] are the objects of activity inherent in linguistic usage.

Thus, even in sentences such as "Devadatta cooks rice in a pot with firewood," which concern objects that are past, future, or present, the relation of a word whose meaning is not yet established is understood through its juxtaposition with words whose meanings are well-known.

Likewise, even from grammar, etymology, lexicography, and philology, the derivation of word-meanings is more explicit; yet in these, there is no comprehension of the meaning as a "thing-to-be-done" (kāryārthatā), because such is not perceived.
But how, then, is the capacity [of words] for their own meanings understood when they are combined in injunctions and the like?

Because injunctions and the like possess the form of a sentence, and since in all cases the word's own meaning is invariably associated with the meanings of other words denoted by the constituent terms, one understands the combined meaning from a word whose relationship has been grasped in that manner.
Therefore, the capacity [of a word] is not established by necessity as being connected with the effect.
Furthermore:
if the meaning of a word were that which is connected with the effect, then because the connection would have to be grasped for each [word] individually...
There would be a loss of verbal authority (*śābdapramāṇa*), for no comprehension of the relationship [between word and meaning] occurs regarding that which is not perceived.

From the Vedic sentence "One desiring heaven should sacrifice," there is no attainment of the cognition of a novel object (*apūrva*), because at the time of knowing the relationship between the two words denoting the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*) and the object of the injunction (*viṣaya*), the person to be enjoined and the object are already established as being conjoined with the task (*kārya*). In that case, the word would be a mere restatement (*anuvāda*) regarding the injunction (*niyoga*) as excluded from the object and the person to be enjoined.
For the relationship between the object and the person to be impelled (niyojya) is not verbal; rather, it is based on the actual state of affairs (artha).

However, when [the word] is connected with something else, the cognition of a new object (apūrvārtha)—such as the knowledge of fire from smoke—is justified through the employment of an indicator (upalakṣaṇa).

It might be argued: since the very task (kārya) that is not yet understood becomes the object of the knowledge of the relationship, the word is not a mere restatement (anuvāda) regarding a task that is excluded from both the object and the person to be impelled.

This is not sound, because if the effect were not understood, then since other objects associated with it would also not be understood, it would follow as an undesirable consequence that all words would convey their meanings even when their relationship [to those meanings] has not been grasped;
for the knowledge of a relationship does not occur when the object is unknown.
Now, it might be argued that in cases such as commands and the like, the object which is the effect is also understood as being reflected through the limiting adjuncts (upādhi).

Nevertheless, since all objects associated with the essential nature [of a word] are already apprehended through other means of knowledge for the sake of knowing their relations, the status of words as mere restatements (*anuvādaka*) is established. Now, if it is argued that the meaning of a word is the impeller (*pravartaka*) because it is grasped by another means of knowledge, yet the specific impeller—the *niyoga* (injunction)—is cognized as distinguished from the object and the person to be enjoined; even so, the verbal relation would be a restatement, while the specific element would fall within the scope of residual inference (*pariśeṣānumāna*), and thus there would be no attainment of the cognition of a new object (*apūrvārtha*). Therefore, the establishment of a new object occurs when the relation is grasped as being "connected with another" (*anyānvita*), by employing a qualifier (*upalakṣaṇa*).
Furthermore:

"The state of being the counter-correlate of the relation does not belong to the object of inference in its entirety; let it not be the case that [the relation] serves as a means of cognition in another way, for those two [means] would then be equal. (49)

If even the "effect" (kārya), which is being followed as it is inferred from the activity [of usage] during the comprehension of the word's capacity whose object is the cognition induced by that activity, were to be postulated as the regulator for the scope of the capacity of all words, then—since [the property of] being cognized by another means of knowledge exists in some cases while it is absent in others, and since the knowledge of the relation [between word and meaning] arises from usage and cognition when it exists and does not arise when it is absent—that [property] too would become a regulator for the scope of the capacity of all words.

But surely, having inferred the motivating cognition through the activity [of the subject], one understands the capacity of the word in that very [cognition]; so how is there room for the necessity of being cognizable by another means of knowledge (*pramāṇāntara*) and so forth?
True—let it be so in this particular application; however, in other applications involving different relations, one must seek out a common factor (*prayojaka*) that persists throughout.
But surely, the "thing to be done" (*kārya*) persists everywhere.
It is true that there is also a recurrence (anuvṛtti) of "being cognizable by other means of knowledge" and so forth, due to the rule of positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka).
But was it not already explained that "being cognizable by other means of knowledge" and the like do not fall within the scope of the word's own expressive power (śabda-sāmarthya)?
In that case, let it be postulated that the expressive power resides in its own meaning as connected with an effect characterized by "being measured by other means of knowledge" and so forth.
[Objection: Surely, that which persists when there is the capacity of a word [to denote] its object is precisely what is the motivator (prayojaka).

[Reply: That is not so; rather than such a qualification, it is better to grasp the persisting factor as the motivator. [Objection: Surely, since it is known through other means of cognition (mānāntara), it is better to grasp it as "connected with an effect" (kāryānvita) rather than as "connected with an action characterized by being cognized through other means."
It is true that even more easily grasped than that is the apprehension of the capacity [of words] as being possessed of a concomitance (*anvaya*).

But surely, since the positive and negative concomitances (*anvaya-vyatireka*) of being measured by another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and so forth are understood to be established otherwise (*anyathāsiddha*) as means for grasping the relationship [between word and meaning], they do not lead to the understanding of the capacity of all words as being restricted to their respective objects. This is because when a word is employed with the intention of expressing a certain thing, and the knowledge of the sentence-meaning is inferred from the resulting activity [of the listener], the relationship is understood; whereas it is not understood otherwise. Therefore, the positive and negative concomitances do not indicate that the capacity of every word is restricted to its specific object.

In that case, since activity is established only when there is knowledge of the effect, one would infer the knowledge of the sentence-meaning and, from that, know the word's capacity; otherwise, due to the absence of such knowledge, the positive and negative concomitances (anvaya-vyatireka) of the word would be established as otherwise-accounted for, and thus they would not lead to the conclusion that the word’s capacity is restricted to the domain of all [other] word-meanings.
Therefore, the capacity [of a word] resides in being connected with something else.

Now, if it is argued that even though [properties] such as being an effect possess positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka), their status as determiners of the scope of a word’s semantic capacity is abandoned and they are established otherwise as mere means—then let it be said that the relation (saṃsarga) itself lacks the status of being the object of a word’s semantic capacity.
This is not sound.

For one must state that the cognition of that [relation] is established otherwise by relying either on a sentence distinct from the words, or on the relations between the word-meanings already awakened by the words, which serve as the causes of that [cognition].

Furthermore, because the assumption of power (*śakti*) for both of those two positions involves the fault of conceptual complexity (*gaurava*), and because there is no connection with the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding the objects themselves as being the locus of that power—as has been described—the cognition of relation is postulated to be based solely on words.
Moreover: if the meaning of a word were [only] that which is connected to an action (*kārya*), with what would the action itself be connected?

Words such as "quality" (guṇa) or "substance" (dravya) have no direct connection with the action to be accomplished (kārya). To avoid the dual nature—where words other than the word for the action possess the capacity to denote that which is connected to the action, while the word for the action itself possesses the capacity either in its own form or when connected to something else—one must adopt only a single determinant: the capacity to denote that which is connected to something else. This is because an action cannot be connected to another action. Even for one who states the determinant to be "the capacity to denote that which is connected to what is connected to the action"—which is like the "crane-catching" (bakabandha) method—he incurs the fault of having a determinant with too many qualifications.

Even one who, having accepted that the capacity [of words] resides in their connection with what is fit and unfit, restricts fitness by asserting that the connection of the others is possible only for the sake of the task (kārya), and that the task’s connection is with the others—by such a person, the mutual fitness for connection among qualities, substances, factors of action (kāraka), and so forth, which is established by perception, must not be denied.

If it is argued: "True, that fitness is objective (ārthī), but the verbal (śābdī) fitness belongs only to the task and the other word-meanings"—we say no, because qualities, substances, factors of action, and so forth, are not directly fit for connection with the meaning of the task-word.
For there is a fixed rule: the connection of the task is with the meaning of the verbal root (bhāvārtha), whereas the factor of action connects with the meaning of the verbal root.

Now, it may be thought that the immediate connection (*anvaya*) among all things, characterized by the relationship of subordinate and principal (*śeṣa-śeṣitā*), is based on their purpose (*kārya*), whereas the connection characterized by action and its factors (*kriyā-kāraka*) is mediated. But what is this "subordinate-principal" relationship? It cannot be the status of servant and master, because that pertains only to sentient beings. If it is argued that "being subordinate" (*taccheṣatā*) consists in the necessity of being performed (*kartavyatā*) under the condition (*upādhi*) of that [principal], we say no; for universals (*jāti*), qualities (*guṇa*), and substances (*dravya*) lack such necessity, as they are established entities (*siddha-rūpa*).
Nor is there a relationship of substrate and superstrate, or of subordinate and principal, as in the case of a quality and its possessor.
If it is argued that it is a relationship of beneficiary and benefactor,
then the meaning of the verbal root (bhāvārtha) alone would be the principal of the other word-meanings.

Even a slave born in the house (*garbhadāsa*), when being benefited by his master, is a *śeṣin* (the principal); however, by virtue of the relationship of service (*bhṛtyatva*), he is subordinate (*guṇabhūta*) through that other connection.
Now, what constitutes predominance (*prādhānya*)? Is it by virtue of the word (*śabda*) or by virtue of the meaning (*artha*)?

If [the capacity for connection] were based on verbal expression (*śabda*), then because curds alone possess primacy, the verbal connection would pertain to the necessity of performing the oblation as qualified by those curds.

If it were based on the meaning (*artha*), then primacy belongs only to that which is to be assisted (the beneficiary), and since that [beneficiary-ship] belongs to the efficient force (*bhāvārtha*) without mediation, whereas pleasure or the cessation of suffering belongs only through mediation, there would be no fixed rule regarding the fitness for connection with the task (*kārya*).

Therefore, it is most appropriate to hold that the capacity of words lies in their connection with a fit [object], in accordance with the fitness established by other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Furthermore:
There is no need for supplying an ellipsis (adhyāhāra) nor for inference (anumā) regarding the cognition of an existing object;
because of the complexity of conceptual construction (kalpanā-gaurava), let its capacity be accepted on the basis of observing the effect. || 51 ||

To begin with, worldly cognition of an existing entity (*bhūtārtha*) based on a word is not a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*), because one understands the existing entity from the word—just as one does from perception and so forth—and then, recollecting its status as a cause of benefit or harm, engages in non-contradictory practical activity (*vyavahāra*).

Now, if it is argued that even in that case a "thing to be done" (*kārya*) is superimposed [upon the word], we reply: first of all, there can be no superimposition of a "thing to be done" inherent in the object itself, because the cognizer would not understand the intention regarding engagement or withdrawal in relation to that object.

Nor can there be the ellipsis "it is to be known," because in the case of "it is to be known that Devadatta has gone out," since the cognition arises from the two words alone regarding either the essential nature of the referent—the going out of Devadatta—or its relation [to Devadatta], there would be no connection between the words characterized by semantic competency (*yogyatā*), as the required effect would already have been accomplished with respect to its object.

But when [the act] is enjoined as something yet unarisen, there can be no production of the cognition of Devadatta’s departure; for the two feet [of the injunction] lack the power to produce that [cognition], because the injunctive word (*vidhipada*) serves as the cause of the cognition regarding the duty to perform the cognition of Devadatta’s departure, and because the cognition that is to be enjoined is distinct from the cognition of the object of the injunction.
Therefore, if one were to supply the words "is to be known" (*jñātavyaḥ*), the consequence would be the loss of the actual valid cognition (*bhūtapramiti*).

Furthermore, rather than postulating an additional causal factor—that it must be an "effect"—in order to understand the relationship [between word and meaning], and thus assuming the insertion of an unperceived word in every sentence in common usage, it is better to postulate that the capacity [of words] resides in their being connected [with other meanings].
Now, if it is argued that worldly cognition of an actual state of affairs is not verbal but rather based on inference—

this is not so, because even in that case, there would be the conceptual complexity (kalpanā-gaurava) of abandoning the word, just as one does in the case of positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka). Nor is there an establishment of the inference of a connection between actual states of affairs from words capable of expressing a connection with what is to be accomplished (kārya-saṃsṛṣṭa-samartha-śabda).
Nor is this an error of association, because—unlike a perceptual illusion—it is not sublated and it does not contradict worldly practice.

Furthermore, since the function of a word is observed to apply to that which is associated with another [meaning], its capacity is postulated as residing in that much alone, for capacity is understood through its effect.
But one might object: if there is no apprehension of the capacity in that much alone, how can the effect be observed there?

This is not a fault; for even at the time of knowing the relationship, the state of being connected with another [object] exists by virtue of being included within the connection with the *kārya* (the thing to be accomplished).

However, it is only through the observation of the *kārya* that the capacity is restricted to that much alone. But [one might object]: if the motivator (*prayojaka*) has not been determined, how can there be the production of the *kārya*?

Even for one who does not postulate another instigator, since the effect of cognition is observed from a sentence denoting an action (*kārya*), the occurrence of the effect of cognition is equally possible under the view that [words denote] being conjoined with something else (*anyānvita*), because at the time of knowing the relationship, the action itself is also present. Therefore, it is established that the capacity [of words] does not reside in being conjoined with an action, but rather in being conjoined with something else.

Having accepted that words such as *liṅga* (the optative suffix) denote the action to be performed (*kārya*), it was stated that their capacity to signify [an object] as connected with another arises from the power of the instigator (*prayojaka*) and the material cause (*upādāna*).

Now, in order to demonstrate that this very [denotation of the action to be performed] does not exist, he says: "In the case of an illustration, there is no other cause for specific linguistic usage."

For the status of being a task (*kāryatva*) is understood as being established otherwise than from the means to a desired end (*iṣṭābhyupāya*). That which has been apprehended by one desiring to learn as the cause for his own activity is inferred to be the very same cause for the activity of the learner as well; and that [cause] is not apprehended as anything other than the cognition of the means to a desired end.
But surely, one also engages in action based on the knowledge of the result?
True; however, that engagement, which has that [knowledge] as its cause, is characterized solely by desire (*icchā*), and not by a specific nature consisting of bodily activity and the like.
For that [bodily activity] is the basis for inferring an instigator in others, because it falls within the range of perception.
And this [activity] is caused solely by the knowledge of the means for accomplishing what is desired in such a manner.

Even when one proceeds at some time with a desire to know its specific details after having gained knowledge of the means in general, it is from that [knowledge of the means] alone that one proceeds, not from the mere knowledge of the result.
Now, one might object: even a desired means, if understood as being in the past or another such state, does not incite activity.
True. His knowledge of the connection with time is an obstacle to activity.

But surely, the status of something as a cause is established only when an obstacle is postulated? True. However, when an agent understands that a means is conducive to what he desires yet lacks the knowledge of its connection with time—and fails to act when that [knowledge] is not understood—the fact that this knowledge is indeed the cause of activity is apprehended through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) arising from the non-occurrence of both positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*).
[Objection: But surely, even when that [cognition] exists, one who lacks the capacity does not act.

[Response: True. However, since it is from the cognition of a specific object—given the completeness of the means such as the agent’s capability—that one acts, that very [cognition] must be admitted by the proponent of the "thing-to-be-done" (*kāryavādin*) as the cause of activity, because it is precisely there that the rule of dependence upon the word applies.

[Objection: Even so, it has been stated that what prompts action is the cognition of the "thing-to-be-done" as a means to the agent's desired end, distinguished by time and characterized by its suitability for volitional effort (*kṛti*).
In that case, why should the status of being an "effect" (*kārya*) alone not be the cause for engagement?
We reply: because engagement is not invariably concomitant with the fruit (*phala*).

For even that [fruit], whether it be pleasure or the cessation of pain, is understood to be an "effect" by virtue of its fitness for volitional effort (*kṛti-yogyatā*), either directly or through mediation.
It has been stated that in that case, the specific activity characterized by desire is not [the cause].
If so, then the state of being an effect (kāryatva) residing in the means to what is beneficial is itself the cause of activity.
That is not so, because it cannot be logically predicated as a qualifier.

[Objection: But surely, since [the cognition] does not incite activity even toward things like past fire which are means to a benefit, the fitness for action (*kṛtiyogyatā*) must also necessarily be required.

[Reply: No; for even the cognition of an accomplished portion of an object—which has as its content a means to what is desired either directly or indirectly—is a cause of activity regarding that portion of the object. However, just like the causal capacity of the means, the fitness for action of the object is also required as a subordinate factor in the activity. Primacy, however, belongs to the being a means to a benefit alone; for even when there is fitness for action, if the state of being a means to a benefit is absent, no specific activity is observed.

[Objection: But since the positive and negative concomitances (anvaya-vyatireka) are equally present for the effect as well, why should the effect itself not be considered the primary [cause]? [Response:

No, because the positive and negative concomitances can be accounted for otherwise (*anyathāsiddhi*) by their being characterized by a temporal sequence and by their fitness for action (*kṛti-yogyatā*), which serves to remove any obstacle.
[Objection: Surely, it is better to postulate the status of being a cause than to postulate the removal of an obstacle.
That is not so;

for when one cause exists, another cause is postulated on the basis of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) that cannot be otherwise accounted for (*ananyathāsiddha*). And it has been stated that those two [concomitances] are otherwise accounted for.
Is this temporal connection (*kālopabandha*) an obstruction (*pratibandha*), or rather the absence of a cause?

It is indeed an obstruction; for even when the established cause—the status of being a means to a desired end (*hitasādhanatva*)—is present there as well, it acts as an obstacle to the effect of activity because it is incompatible with that effect, and because the status of being an effect (*kāryatā*) has not yet been established.
But if this were so, would there not be a loss of the material cause (*upādāna*) and the auxiliary causes (*sahakāri-kāraṇa*) in all cases?

It would not be so. Where there is a positive concomitance (*anvaya*) of something through the exclusion of another entity that is incompatible with the effect, there its concomitance occurs precisely through the removal of an impediment.

However, where there is a positive concomitance of something with the effect—established through both positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*)—by way of excluding its own mere absence, there its concomitance occurs precisely as a cause.
In this case, however, the cognition of temporal restriction is another entity that is incompatible with purposeful activity (*pravṛtti*).
And that [notion] is set aside by the cognition of being an effect.

Furthermore, the positive concomitance (anvaya) of the potter and so forth is not established merely through the exclusion of other opposing lumps of clay; rather, it is established precisely as a cause, because even when that [potter] is absent in some cases, the jar does not arise.
In this case, however, the cognition of a means to a desired end, being temporally distinct, necessarily produces activity provided that the causal capacity is present.

But surely, it might be argued: "Is it not to be postulated that the effect itself is the cause of activity, its connection with a fruit is an obstacle to activity, and the removal of that obstacle is the state of being a means to what is desired?
For we observe that no activity occurs toward suffering or its causes—even though they are capable of being produced by an effort—if they lack the status of being a means to what is beneficial.
Furthermore, in those two cases as well, [the obstacle] is simply the state of being an impediment to activity."
For even in the case of a mere entity that is not empty of both [aspects] and is capable of being produced, one does not observe activity.
Now, if it is argued that even this [mere entity] acts as an obstacle to activity because it causes some degree of suffering by virtue of being an object of activity, [we reply:
no, for activity occurs only after that very thing has been understood to be a means to a desired end.
Now, the knowledge that something is not a means for achieving welfare everywhere acts as an obstacle to activity.
For if there were no certainty regarding absence in the case of a non-perception of what is otherwise capable, there would be activity toward a mere entity whose nature is simply fit for production.
Now, being an effect does not consist merely in fitness for production; rather, it is fitness for the undertaking of action by one who acts with prior intelligence.
And that [desire] is directed toward the beneficial or the means to achieve it, and not elsewhere.
Therefore, the result itself is the obstacle to activity, while its being a means to that [result] is what removes that obstacle.

If so, for one who acts with deliberation, the desirability inherent in the object—which is fit to be projected as an action—is either the state of being desired as distinct from the mere fitness for accomplishment, or its being a means to that [result]; nothing else, because no other [definition] can be established.
If it is argued that [desire] is the opposite of the absence of activity—no, for it would follow that activity itself is the motivator.

If it is argued that being the motivator consists in being the opposite of the absence of activity—then desire alone is that [motivator]; "oughtness" (*kartavyatā*), however, is inherent in the object.
Or rather, it is the beneficial and so forth that is the opposite of the absence of activity.

In that case, since the beneficial [object] itself lacks the status of being a specific cause for engagement, it is simply the means to the beneficial that is designated by another term as the cause of engagement; thus, this is not a different position.

We, however, maintain only this much: that it is precisely the capacity of the means to the beneficial to be accomplished that is required—either as an instrument or by way of removing obstacles—to engagement.
But surely, even regarding a means to a means, one engages because of knowledge concerning that object?
True. Having accepted that the means is beneficial through a succession [of steps], one proceeds toward its accomplishment;
thus, while the activity directed toward the immediate means is characterized simply by desire, the activity toward the means of that means is indeed distinguished.
This being so, the injunctions regarding the auxiliary rites such as the *prayāja* accept that they are beneficial to the sacrifice itself and thereby enjoin their status as its very instruments.

Or, even if the "task-to-be-done" (*kāryatā*) residing in the means to achieve a desired end (*hitasādhana*) is the cause of activity, nevertheless, "task-to-be-done" is not the meaning of the word. For instance, when a cognizer understands the "task-to-be-done" residing in the means to the desired end through the inferential mark of activity, the cognition of the "task-aspect" characterized by suitability for accomplishment is established by inference from the mere understanding of the nature of the action constituting the primary meaning of the verbal root. Therefore, the expressive power of the suffixes such as *liṅ* is postulated to reside in the aspect of being a means to the desired end; otherwise, it would be illogical for that which is already established [by other means] to be the meaning of the word.

Furthermore, at that time, the fact that bringing a cow is a means to achieve a desired end is not understood through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), because the production of the result is not yet observed.

Nor can it be established by inference, because the nature of the action as a means to the desired object is subject to deviation, and because the mere capacity for accomplishment—which is independent of temporal constraints—is not invariably present in the essential form of the action itself.
Therefore, it is established that the meaning of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and other such suffixes, as the cause of engagement, is precisely that which is a means to the agent's desired end.
On this point, someone says: Is the bringing of the cow a means to achieve what the agent desires by its own nature, or because it is commanded?

If it were by its own nature, then one who recalls the bringing of the cow would spontaneously engage in it through an inference that the action possesses the quality of being a means to a benefit, as observed in previously established instances of bringing cows.

If, however, it is because it is commanded, then in the Veda there would be no establishment of the primary meaning as a means to a benefit, since there is an absence of being commanded [in the case of the eternal Vedic text].
And the absence of that [human authorship] in the Veda is due to its being non-human (apauruṣeya). To this, he says:
"The status of being a means [of knowledge] is self-established; however, for a particular [instance], it is like an effect."
Even the agent intends the door that is considered primary.
In this regard, you too must be questioned: is the bringing of the cow a task by its own nature, or is it so by virtue of being commanded?
If it were by its own nature, then, as in the other case, one would simply perform it oneself upon recollecting that the task of bringing the cow has been accomplished elsewhere.

If it is argued that because the object to be accomplished (*kārya*) is unfit for other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), it cannot be understood from anything else, and thus there is no activity without a word—then in that case, there would be no utterance by the speaker.
For this very reason, there would also be no activity on the part of the listener, since the meaning is not apprehended from a word that has not been uttered.
Furthermore, if [the Veda] were [understood] as a command (*ājñapta*), there would be an absence of the coloring of the object-to-be-accomplished (*kāryoparāga*).

Since the status of being a task (*kāryatā*) is established by the very fact of being commanded, there is no need to postulate the expressive power (*śabdasāmarthya*) of the word in that regard. For if [the status of being a task] were due to the coloring (*uparāga*) by a command, then it would follow that such a status would be absent in cases such as requests (*adhyeṣaṇā*) and in the Veda. Now, if it is argued that "coloring by a task" is merely coloring by whatever prompts action (*pravartaka*); [we reply:]...
And whether that [activity] is based on one's own impulse or on the instigation, request, or permission of another, the aforementioned fault applies in both cases.
Now, if it is argued that for a child, the bringing of the cow toward his own activity is not the "task" (kārya) in its own form, but rather as conditioned by the fulfillment of what he desires;
likewise, even though the bringing of the cow is not the object of the [speaker's] verbal application, it becomes the task because it fulfills what is desired by himself.
And that [action] desired by the agent of the command and so forth is accomplished for the agent as well, by way of accomplishing what is desired by him.
Therefore, it is precisely the specific act of bringing the cow that is, by implication, colored by the "task" (kārya) for the agent.

And this is understood from the word itself; for since the mere act of bringing the cow can deviate from accomplishing what is desired by the agent, it is impossible to apprehend its status as a "task" through inference, and thus it is impossible to know its coloring by the task through that means.
In that case, let it be understood from the instruction itself that this very [act] possesses such a capacity for accomplishing a benefit.

And let the fact that this specific act of bringing the cow is a means to a beneficial end be postulated as being caused by the nature of the agent, just as the status of being a "task" (*kāryatva*) is.

Thus, the use of words such as the optative suffix (*liṅ*) occurs with respect to a means characterized or qualified by such a result; just as the use of the optative suffix occurs with respect to a task characterized or indicated by the agent's volition (*kṛti*), or just as the word "this" (*idam*) is used with respect to a jar or similar object qualified or indicated by its being present before one.
But surely the speaker intends to express the bringing of the cow as a means to achieve his own desired end, not as a means to achieve the agent's desired end.
In that case, how can there be the employment of a word for what is a means to the agent's desired end?
And if it is not so employed, how can there be knowledge of the relationship [between the word and its meaning] with respect to that?
This objection does not hold, for it applies equally even to the case of an action (*kārya*).

For the speaker employs speech in order to have another accomplish what is to be done by himself; he does not employ it with the intention of expressing what is to be done by the person being directed. In that case, how could the word’s capacity [to produce activity] reside in the action of the one being directed? For one does not set out to act toward the action of another.
Surely, in an instruction (upadeśa), it is precisely the duty of the instigator (prayojaka) that is intended to be expressed.
Likewise, even the status of being a means to a beneficial end (hitasādhanatā) is intended to be expressed in an instruction directed toward the person to be prompted (prayojya).

Now, if in cases such as commands (praiṣa) and the like, the instigator intends to express that the accomplishment of his own duty is also the duty of the person to be prompted, then the instigator indeed intends to express a means to the desire of the agent through a causal chain: namely, that he brings about what is desired by the person to be prompted, which is itself the accomplishment of what is desired by himself.

Therefore, just as even in the case of an effect postulated by others, one observes the engagement of the agent and—inferring that he possesses a cognition of his own duty—grasps the relationship [between the word and the object] therein, since engagement arises precisely from the cognition of one's own effect; so too it is in the case of the cognition of the means to a desired end. We perceive no difference between the two. [Objection: But surely the initial activity of a newborn creature, such as the placement of hands and feet, does not arise from a cognition of the means to a beneficial end, because that [cognition] is to be inferred from the production of its fruit.
[Reply: But then, from what does the cognition of the effect itself arise?
It will be stated that [the self] is not known through perception;
nor is it known through inference and the like, due to the absence of knowledge of a [logical] connection.
Now, if it is argued that such activity is not preceded by cognition, then no cause need be sought.
The same applies to the other case as well.

Now, if it is argued that [the inclination] arises from the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) of the knowledge of an effect belonging to another birth—then why should it not arise from a similar latent impression of the knowledge of the means to what is desired?
Therefore, it is established that activity proceeds from that very [latent impression].
Now, what indeed is this so-called "being a means to a beneficial end"?
Is it the mere nature of the thing itself, or is it a property of that thing?
It cannot be the mere nature, because that is accessible through perception, whereas its status as a means is not apprehended in that way.
"It is not a property (dharma), because there is no means of valid cognition for its existence. To this, he replies:
"There is valid cognition for the excellence of the object through positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka)."
Otherwise, how could there be linguistic usage regarding things employed by others?

(54) Even though the intrinsic nature of the object remains the same, a certain excellence in its capacity as a means is postulated because the production of the result would otherwise be inexplicable.

But is it not the case that the production of the result arises from that which has become the object of activity, while activity arises from that which is inferred to be a means because of the production of the result; thus, there is mutual dependence?
Nor can it be understood that [the means] possesses the status of being a means simply from seeing a result produced by an object that has been made the focus of another's activity;
otherwise, how could there be for anyone the practical engagement characterized by the appropriation of something specifically for the sake of a desired result?
Therefore, this excellence (atiśaya) certainly exists.

But surely, since the optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and others have their relationship established with various intentions such as commands (*praiṣa*), how could they express the state of being a means to one's welfare?
[Reply: No, because that expression is observed in the case of instruction (*upadeśa*).
[Objection: But even there, favor (*anugraha*) is what is expressed.

Even in the absence of that [actual performance], it is not out of fear of the unseen (adṛṣṭa) that the capacity for accomplishing a beneficial end is intended by the instruction; rather, this is shown to be the intended meaning even in the case of commands and the like through a traditional succession. Furthermore, since activity does not arise from mere commands and the like when there is knowledge of the relationship [between word and object] regarding the cause of action, that [relationship] alone is the meaning of the word, and not the command itself. This is because, in the case of those [commands], the relationship is not known, there is no observed instance for a child, and because commands and the like are established otherwise—as being inferable from signs such as the excellence or deficiency of the speaker and the listener, or facial expressions and so forth.
Furthermore:
Because activity arises from passion (rāga) and the like, since those [desire for results] are its causes, it is not an effect [of words].
And the passion that is the cause of activity is not derived from verbal testimony, because it is established by direct perception. (55)
Is it not the case that the very cognition of passion as being an effect is the cause?
No; for since passion arises when there is something desired and fails to arise when there is nothing desired, the desired object itself is its immediate cause.

[Objection: But surely, since the cognition of the desired object arises first and passion follows from that, the cognition is "otherwise established" (anyathāsiddha) as being merely the cause of the cause.

That is not so. If "being an effect" (*kāryatā*) is the fitness to be made the object of an effort (*kṛti*), then that is established—by means of an inference based on the example of an action already accomplished by oneself, which lacks knowledge of a connection with time—simply from the cognition of the nature of the action characterized as the meaning of the verbal root; it does not depend upon the cognition of it being a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhana*). Alternatively, if "being an effect" is the fitness to be projected by an effort belonging to one who acts with prior deliberation, then that [fitness] would consist in its being desired or its being a means to that [desired end]; thus, it is said that desire arises precisely from the desired and so forth.

Even if one were to postulate that some third factor is the objective support for the cognition of it as an effect, nevertheless, since both desire and the cognition of it as an effect would arise from the very same cause—namely, the beneficial object and so forth—the beneficial object would not be the "cause of the cause" of desire. This is because even when a plantain fruit or the like, which is a means to a benefit, has already been produced, it becomes an object of desire by virtue of being qualified by the act of eating; otherwise, there would be no distinction even if one were to postulate that desire arises from the cognition of the beneficial object, and the cognition of it as an effect arises from the cognition of desire.
[Objection: But could it not be the case that the comprehension of something as a means to a benefit depends upon the cognition of it as an effect?

Since there is no other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for its being an effect, whereas for its being a means (*sādhanatā*), the impossibility of the production of a result otherwise has been stated, and as for the result itself, its favorability is established by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

Furthermore, since the cognition of "what is to be done" (*kāryabuddhi*) is invariably restricted to that very place where there is the state of being beneficial and a means thereto, it is postulated that this [state] alone is the cause thereof.

Therefore, having inferred the instigating passion (*rāga*) in the agent by the sign of his activity, and because that [passion], being self-evident, does not depend on words, it is postulated that the capacity of the word resides in the knowledge of its being a means to the beneficial—which is the cause of that [passion]; thus, it is well-reasoned.
Furthermore, this cognition of what is to be done (kārya-buddhi) is examined as to what it rests upon:

the cognition of what is to be done does not rest upon an injunction (niyoga), nor upon that which is to be accomplished (niṣpādya), nor upon an effort devoid of attachment (kṛti-rakta), nor upon a goal to be achieved (sādhya) that is free from conditions (nirupādhika), nor even upon something distinguished by time (kālataḥ). (56)
It does not apprehend what is unprecedented, nor does it [apprehend] primordial matter (pradhāna) with respect to an action;
its status as an instigator is not contradicted by non-existence, because of deviation.
The phrase "because of deviation" is connected to every [preceding case].
The cognition of the "task" (kārya) does not, in the first place, depend upon an injunction (niyoga).
For an injunction is well known as a particular intention characterized by the instigation of a primary conscious being toward a subordinate conscious being.

And that [intention] deviates from the cognition of the task in the case of a child’s spontaneous activity and in the Veda, because there is an absence of knowledge regarding a connection with such a person.

Nor does it depend merely on the fitness to be the object of an effort (*kṛti*), because that [fitness] exists even in relation to suffering and the like, which are not within the scope of the cognition of what is to be done (*kārya*); thus, there would be a logical deviation (*vyabhicāra*). Nor does it depend on an object conjoined with an effort that is currently being measured, because the arising of an effort is dependent upon the cognition of what is to be done; at the time of the cognition of what is to be done, the conjunction with an effort is absent, and thus there would be a logical deviation. Furthermore, "what is to be done" (*kārya*) is not an unconditioned end (*nirupādhika-sādhya*), since such a status belongs only to pleasure and the like; moreover, we observe the cognition of what is to be done even toward a means that is a conditioned end (*sopādhika-sādhya*).

Furthermore, there is no such thing as an unconditioned (nirupādhika) object of accomplishment apart from the cessation of pleasure and pain. Now, does the cognition of an effect take as its objective support that which is distinct from time,
either by virtue of its verbal expression or by virtue of its actual meaning?

If [the definition of a "cognition of an effect" is based] on the word, then even words such as "jar" do not denote an object connected with time; consequently, the cognitions produced by them would also result in being cognitions of effects. If it is based on the object, then the cognition of a hare's horn would also result in being such a cognition, for that alone is "non-existent" (tuccha) which has not been, does not exist, and will not exist.
But surely, when "an effect" (kārya) is stated, no connection with time is perceived; nevertheless, there is still no apprehension of its being a mere nothingness (tucchatā).
True, it has been said that the non-apprehension of a connection with time through the word itself is equally present even in the cognition produced by the hearing of words such as "jar" (ghaṭa).
But by what means is the distinction of time apprehended from the perspective of the object (arthatas)?
It cannot be by means of the cognition of the effect alone, because that cognition is restricted solely to that [effect].
Nor can it be that very same cognition which establishes the emptiness of time as well; for we do not know to what it would belong.
If you say "to the effect," we reply no, because that very effect is what is currently being investigated.
If it is argued that the object is "distinct from time"—then, since such an object is either time or a void, how can there be a distinction from the void?

Furthermore, by one who maintains that an effect is distinct from the void, a connection with time must be asserted for it in reality, even if it lacks [temporal] cognition, just as in the case of jars and the like, because of the inference of a connection with time.
Moreover, even the "unprecedented" (*apūrva*) cannot be the objective basis [of the notion of duty], because it deviates from the cognition of ordinary worldly effects.
Nor is that possible even in the Veda, because there is a lack of evidence.
If it is argued that the necessity of performing a sacrifice for one who desires heaven (*svargakāmin*) would otherwise be inexplicable—[we reply that] that very necessity is itself not established;
and it has already been stated that it is not a mandate (*niyoga*) or the like.
If it is asked what inconsistency there is in [the sacrifice] being a means to heaven without the *apūrva*, [the answer is:
since a sacrifice perishes in a moment, its status as a means to a result occurring at a later time is untenable.
[Objection: In that case, it is not established by the *apūrva* alone, because of the absence of a specific body and sense organs [to experience the fruit].
That too must be accepted; let it be understood through inference established by common worldly experience.

If, then, the sacrifice’s status as a means to heaven is not contradicted even when the required purpose is fulfilled—since the accomplishment of the fruit arises from the Lord, who is woven together by hundreds of Śruti and Smṛti texts, depending upon the performance of rites that have already been completed—there is no room for the postulation of an *apūrva* (unseen potency).
Nor can that [apūrva] be the denotation of a word, because it is cognizable only through the non-occurrence of the word's meaning and because its relationship [to the word] has not been apprehended.

Furthermore, the apprehension of the relationship [of denotation] does not occur in that very [word] through the mediation of the "ought-to-be-done" (*kartavyatā*)—which is the meaning of the verbal root expressed by the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so on—or through the mediation of its being a means to that [result], because it is impossible to postulate two distinct denotable meanings to be understood sequentially within a single performance (*prayoga*), such as the postulation of the *apūrva*.

Nor is there any lack of explanatory coherence (*anupapatti*) regarding the mere form of the optative suffix or the meaning expressed by other words, since there is no absence of another denotable meaning [that would require the *apūrva*].
Therefore, neither the *apūrva* nor its denotation should be postulated in the Veda.
Now, with respect to action (*kṛti*), the effect (*kārya*) is primary. What is this primacy?
It is the capacity to be projected toward action by an agent who acts with prior cognition.

In that case, since pleasure, the cessation of pain, or the means thereto constitute the "task" (kārya), there would be a deviation of the notion of "task" with respect to occasional rites (*naimittika*) and the like.
Furthermore, being a mere motivator does not belong to desire alone, because the notion of "task" is absent in that regard;
moreover, it is well known that there is a deviation in the Veda with respect to commands (*praiṣa*) and the like, as well as desired objects (*iṣṭa*).
And it has been stated that neither passion, nor activity, nor the beneficial (hita) and so forth, but something else, is the opposite of the absence of activity. [Objection:
But surely the objective basis (ālambana) should be postulated through the very capacity of the cognition of what is to be done (kārya-buddhi). [Reply: True;
nothing other than this is postulated, since the literal meaning of the word is possible as merely the fitness to be the object of volitional effort (kṛti).
But surely, when "the task to be accomplished" (kārya) is mentioned, something that has the nature of an instigator is also perceived as being implicitly contained within it.
True; that is precisely the fact of being a means to a desired end (hitasādhanatva), which is characterized by the object’s fitness for being projected as an action.
But surely, the fact of being a means to a desired end is not perceived in the cognition of the task to be accomplished.
It is not so; for that [desire] is also understood as being implicitly contained within the motivating cognition (*pravartaka-buddhi*).

Alternatively, since no objective support (*ālambana*) distinct from the accomplishment of what is beneficial and the like can be determined, the insistence that "this is to be done"—which takes the form of a motivator and has the means to achieve benefit as its object—is merely passion (*rāga*), just as in the thought, "May this be mine. It is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), because the causes of a valid means of knowledge are absent.
How so?
There is no valid cognition [of the Veda] through perception, because it is non-existent [to the senses]; nor is there inference from words;

nor is there presumptive testimony (arthāpatti). Therefore, the notion that "desire is the effect" is not a valid cognition. (58) First of all, the fact that another person's [action], such as the bringing of a cow and so forth, or even a jar and the like, which are perceived as having their own specific nature, has that [Veda] as its cause is not determined by perception.

If it is argued that because the bringing of a cow and so forth are present, they lack the status of being an effect (*kārya*) therein and thus are not perceptible—then, in that case, when the bringing of a cow and so forth are not present, the object of the effect (*kāryārtha*) which depends upon them is even less perceptible, since it is not apprehended independently.
Now, is it not the case that actions such as going are not perceptible, but rather inferable?
By what mark (*liṅga*)? By the occasional conjunctions and disjunctions of a substance that was previously stationary.

For instance, an effect produced by conjunction and disjunction is seen to be occasional and to be preceded by a specific excellence (*atiśaya*) characterized by the conjunction and disjunction of its own substratum.
Likewise, conjunction and disjunction themselves, being occasional, are preceded by a specific excellence of their own substrata.
That which is this specific excellence, being the cause of conjunction and disjunction, is *kriyā* (action).
This is not sound.
That action must either be occasional with respect to its own substrate or not;

for if it were not, the consequence would be the eternality of conjunction and disjunction, which would lead to the fallacy of the reason "because of being occasional" being unestablished (*asiddha*).
If that [action] is occasional, does it precede an excellence (atiśaya) in its own substratum or not?
If it does not, then the reason is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) with respect to that [substratum].

If it does precede an excellence, then because of an infinite regress (*anavasthā*), there would follow the consequence that the locus characterized by conjunction and disjunction cannot be established.

If it is argued that there is no proof for a beginningless succession—[we reply: no, because for that which has not been born from the beginning, the production of the first action is impossible due to the lack of connection with any excellence (*atiśaya*) other than its own substrate; thus, [the reason] is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) in that case.
For this very reason, even an action residing in another [substrate] is not established by means of conjunction and disjunction [with that first substrate].
Furthermore, even though conjunction and disjunction exist between a hawk and a post, the post does not possess action; therefore, the reason is inconclusive.

If it is argued that the conjunctions and disjunctions with one's own location serve as the cause for inferring action in the possessor of that location—[we reply: no, because in the case of fish and the like whose bodies are held by a strong force [in a current], although conjunctions and disjunctions with their own locations exist in the stream, there is an absence of the cognition of action.

Furthermore, since the cognition "it moves" is a present perception even when [the object] is momentary—as in the case of sound or lightning—it is not logical to claim that this is an inference of a past action based on its effect.
Therefore, action is indeed directly perceived.

Therefore, the object to be accomplished (kāryārtha), which is the substratum of perceptual activity or is independent, is not accessible through perception. For this very reason, because it is impossible to know its relationship [to other things], it is not accessible through verbal testimony or inference. Nor can the necessity of its being the object of purposeful action (pravṛttiviṣayatā) serve as a means of cognition for that object to be accomplished; for the engagement with a specific object is established as being based on a specific means for attaining a desired end—a fact proven by the impossibility of producing a result otherwise—and thus there is no room for postulating a new category such as *apūrva*. Otherwise, if the result were disregarded, there would be no fixed rule as to why one engages in a certain action while refraining from another.
Even when the means exists, activity and non-activity are appropriate because there is no necessity regarding the desire for the result.

Now, it might be argued that even a task (kārya) prompts activity only by way of bringing about a desire, and thus a rule [of necessity] is appropriate. This is not so, because if that [task] is not understood, its capacity to prompt activity by way of bringing about a desire cannot be understood.

The fruit, however, is either pleasure or the cessation of suffering, which is indeed directly perceived. The desire for that [fruit], which is devoid of restriction [to a specific object], is established by one's own experience.
Furthermore, since the production of the fruit would otherwise be inexplicable, the excellence of the means conducive to it is also understood through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*).
And immediately after the knowledge of what is a means to welfare, there arises a desire possessing that same form, which is accessible through one's own experience.
Thus, that which is a means to welfare impels [the agent] toward activity by way of inducing desire.
Now, being a means to a result is itself "that which is to be done" (kāryatā).
There is a disagreement regarding the name.

Now, if it is argued that the result itself is postulated as the means (*sādhana*) because it is what must be accomplished, [we reply: since the status of being a means is possible for a thing already established by perception, one who postulates a different entity and its status as a means commits the fault of conceptual over-elaboration (*kalpanā-gaurava*). This is because even established things such as jars are observed to be means for accomplishing desired actions.
Therefore, since being an effect (*kāryatva*) is not itself the means (*sādhanatā*), it is impossible to deny its status as a means;
consequently, the category of "effect" is not understood through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*).

Therefore, since there is an absence of both means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and objects of cognition (*prameya*), it is established that the inclination toward the form of an instigator—namely, the notion "this is an effect"—is nothing other than passion (*rāga*).

Consequently, even in the Veda, the optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and others, by way of expressing the fact of being a means to a desired end, specifically denote the status of being a means to heaven as presented by the immediately adjacent word.

Furthermore, in the case of occasional rites (*naimittika*) and the like, because there is no mention of desire (*kāma*) and because the mention of the occasion (*nimitta*) is invariably connected [to the rite], they are appropriately understood to denote the specific status of being a means to warding off the undesirable that is constantly sought after, which must be inferred.
Otherwise, the objects [taught] in the Veda would be accidental, because it is established that the Veda has action as its purpose.
A qualification of the person to be enjoined (niyojya) does not connect with the action [if it is not a means to a result].

(Verse 59) If the capacity of the word to signify a means to one's welfare were not postulated, then—since the Veda would be restricted solely to the object of action (kārya) and the status of being a means to a fruit would not be understood—all living beings would, by the mere fact of their birth, be subject to purposes consisting of accidental pleasure and pain.
But surely, it is precisely by the force of the *niyoga* (the injunction) that the verbal root-meaning is understood as a means to the result;
for there is deviation [from this rule] in the case of unauthoritative injunctions and occasional rites (*naimittika*).
Nor is there a contradiction with other means of valid cognition when the *niyoga*—as distinguished from its object and the person enjoined—is cognized from the words of an untrustworthy person.

As for the contradiction regarding the relationship between the goal and the means, it does not obstruct the verbal cognition of the injunction (*niyoga*), because that [contradiction] is non-verbal in nature.

If it is argued that there must be a means to the result in the case of an injunction by a trustworthy person (*āpta*), we say no; such a thing is absent in the Veda because it is not of human origin (*apauruṣeya*).
But surely, the instruction for one desiring [a result] occurs in regard to a means to that desire.

For it is observed that even when something is not the means [to the result], there is the qualification of the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*) by the desire for the result; as, for example, among many people desiring a village who are equally near to the gateway, a host distinguishes the person to be enjoined by a specific qualification known to him to exclude the others, saying, "Let the one desiring a village come.
In that case, coming is not the means to the village.

Now, one might object: "In that instance, the activity is not motivated by the desire for the village, but rather caused by the desire for food; therefore, [the village] is not the means [to the activity]."
This is true even in other cases; [the objection] is equal there as well.
Activity is not caused by the desire for heaven, but rather by the *niyoga* (injunction).
Now, if it were the case that in the case of optional rites (*kāmya*) activity toward the verbal roots were based on desire, then their status as means to that desire would be established.

There is no establishment of [the action] as a means to desire because of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*): [the dependence being that] activity toward an object occurs because it is caused by desire, and when its status as a means to that [desire] is established, activity toward it occurs based on that [status].

[Objection: But surely, since heaven and so forth are understood as things to be accomplished (*sādhya*) due to their connection with desire, the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is connected as the means (*sādhana*) when there is a requirement for a means.
[Response: No, because it would follow that even going and so forth would be a means to that [heaven].
If it is argued that [the connection] does not occur because it is not prescribed—how is it established that only what is prescribed is connected? Because [the action] stands in need of a result.
But this is not so, for there is a deviation in the case of obligatory rites (*nitya*) and the like.
Is it not the case that even there, the avoidance of misfortune is the result?
In that case, some other fruit must be postulated here as well. But surely, when heaven—the thing to be accomplished—is already present, what room is there for another fruit?
