It is said in reply: for when there exists another means of valid cognition (*pramiti-hetu*), the expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) and proximity (*saṃnidhi*) undergo the process of syntactic connection (*saṃsarga*) and the manner of performance (*itikartavyatā*), but they do not themselves bring about the cognition of the connection.
There is no means of valid cognition for this [independent injunction].
For an injunction (niyoga), being restricted solely to its own establishment, is not untenable without a connection between an object and a result.

If it is argued that even an injunction is untenable without a result for what is enjoined, because otherwise activity toward it would be impossible—then, since activity occurs even when an injunction exists simply from the understanding that [the act] is a means to a desired end, that [means] alone is the "injunction" as the meaning of the word; what is the use of an internal, redundant (antargaḍu) injunction?

And it has been stated that because [the injunction] depends on the varying intentions of persons, it cannot possibly exist in the Veda. Now, one might object: since the object (*viṣaya*) and the person to be impelled (*niyojya*) are connected by virtue of their relation to a single injunction, and since there is a mutual connection between them, the heaven—which is a qualification of the person to be impelled—is also connected with the meaning of the verbal root. Furthermore, since such a connection is impossible without a relationship of subordinate and principal, heaven, being that which is to be accomplished (*sādhya*), stands as the primary element. But what, precisely, is this so-called "person to be impelled"?

If it is argued that the one who understands "this is my duty" is the person to be enjoined, then it would follow that even the king himself must be enjoined regarding his own duty. Furthermore, what is this relationship expressed as "this is mine"?

If [the relationship] were that of agent and object to be accomplished, then it would follow that even the king is subject to being enjoined. Furthermore, the relationship characterized by purchase and so forth, which is based on the connection between owner and owned, does not exist here.
Alternatively, the relationship might be that of object and subject.

This is because, in the absence of a difference in intention, there would be no dependence on the object [of the action]. Now, the one who understands the meaning of the task is the *niyojya* (the person to be enjoined), not the enjoiner (*niyoktṛ*), for if it were so, it would follow that even the king [would be the *niyojya*].
Now, it might be argued that the conscious being who is the object of reference (uddeśya) is the one to be enjoined (niyojya).
This is not so, because no relationship can be established with the object of reference.
Even if there were such a person to be enjoined, the desire for heaven would not serve as his qualifying attribute.
A qualification is said to be purposeful only when there is possibility [of application] and non-deviation [from the rule].

First of all, the qualification does not exclude the person as unfit for the injunction (*niyoga*) of the New and Full Moon sacrifices, because the fulfillment of that injunction is already established by the scriptural statement "as long as one lives" (*yāvajjīvam*).
Nor does it serve to exclude connection with others, because even one who does not desire heaven must perform the rite during his lifetime, provided he has avoided the time of dusk.

Even this [desire for heaven] might be an incidental indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) rather than a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), because it is the person alone who is the one to be enjoined (*niyojya*), whereas the desire for heaven lacks the status of being the one to be enjoined.

For the distinction between a qualifier and an incidental indicator arises from their role in determining another related entity, based on whether they are connected to the task to be accomplished (*kārya*) or not.

Therefore, while the injunction (*niyoga*) establishes the relationship between the object and the one to be enjoined, it establishes a relationship with the person alone, and not an incidental indicator relationship with the object.
Alternatively, if there were a [mere] relationship, then even living and so forth would have a relationship with the ritual objective (*viṣaya*).

In that case, if there were a relationship as a subordinate factor (*guṇa*) toward the meaning of the verbal root (*bhāvārtha*), it would follow that living and so forth are auxiliary members (*aṅga*); consequently, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that living and so forth would be extended (*atideśa*) even to the modifications (*vikṛti*) of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*).

If, on the other hand, they were primary, it would follow that living and so forth are themselves things to be accomplished (*sādhya*), which would lead to the consequence that even in an obligatory (*nitya*) rite, there would be the requirement to perform all its auxiliary members (*sarvāṅgopasaṃhāra*).

Furthermore, if desire were a qualification of the person to be enjoined (niyojya), then because of its connection with the injunction, it would—like "living" and so forth—become a causal condition (nimitta); consequently, there would also be sin (pratyavāya) incurred from its non-performance.

Therefore, when it is understood through the verbal suffix (*pratyaya*) that the action is merely a means to a result, and there arises an expectancy for its specific nature, the word *svargakāma*—though primarily denoting a person by virtue of being part of a compound—is connected as the provider of the specific result, because it is directed toward that [result] since heaven is perceived as the object of desire and thus the thing to be accomplished (*sādhya*). Consequently, it is elegant to conclude that one who desires that [heaven] possesses the qualification (*adhikāra*) for that [action].
Now, [one might object]: "By means of finite verbs (*tiṅ*), primary derivatives (*kṛt*), secondary derivatives (*taddhita*), and compounds..."

Because of the qualification "unexpressed" (*anabhihite*), when the instrumentality of the sacrifice has already been expressed by the verbal suffix (*tiṅ*), the instrumental case ending in *jyotiṣṭomena* would be untenable; therefore, he says:
"When not indicated by the verbal suffix or other such means, the instrumental case is not contradicted."
Because the statement of the prohibition [of suffixes] would be redundant, that [restriction] does not apply, since it relies on different meanings. First,
[the rule] "when not already expressed" (anabhihite) does not apply to verbal suffixes (tiṅ), primary derivatives (kṛt), secondary derivatives (taddhita), or compounds (samāsa).

Thus, this prohibition has a perceptible purpose; however, when it is said "the jar is being made" (*ghaṭaḥ kriyate*), since the status of the jar as the object (*karmakārakatva*) is already expressed by both suffixes, the prohibition is intended to prevent that redundancy.

In that regard, just as there is no contingency of tautology even when "Bring the white cow with a long staff" is stated twice—because there is a difference in the aspects of the *kāraka* related to the distinct base-meanings (*prakṛti-artha*)—so too, there is no fault in the expression of each respective *kāraka* by the nominal suffix (*sup*) and the verbal suffix (*tiṅ*), because there is a difference in the aspects of the *kāraka* related to the general and specific base-meanings denoted by the words *yajati* (sacrifices) and *jyotiṣṭoma*. Furthermore, if the verbal suffix did not express the instrumentality (*karaṇatā*), then the prohibition [of the instrumental case] would simply not apply; or rather, this prohibition concerns other types of *kārakas*.

But surely, if the word "desire" (kāmanā) serves to present the fruit, then no one would be established as qualified for the ritual action; furthermore, if the meaning of the sentence were simply the means to the fruit, there would be no distinction between optional (kāmya) and obligatory (nitya) rites. To this, he says: "The qualification belongs to him for whom [the act] is a means to a desired end."
The distinction between optional (*kāmya*) and obligatory (*nitya*) rites arises from the distinction among their qualifying factors.

(61) For whomsoever this rite accomplishes what is desired, for him this rite belongs; thus, through the very act of *niyoga* (the mandate), the relationship of ownership between the person and the rite is established by implication. Once the status of the rite as a benefactor is understood, its ownership [by the performer] is also logically established because it is undertaken for that purpose.

Now, it might be argued that when it is said "one should sacrifice" (*yajeta*), what is understood is "the sacrifice is my duty," and not "the sacrifice is the means to achieve my desired end. This is not so; for even for those who maintain that the injunction (*niyoga*) or the productive operation (*bhāvanā*) is primary, the cognition of the sacrifice as something to be performed arises subsequent to the cognition of the injunction or the productive operation. Therefore, here too, there is no contradiction in the fact that the cognition of being a means to the desired end occurs immediately after [the cognition of the injunction]. Consequently, the agent first understands himself as the owner (*svāmin*) with respect to the action—which is the means to his own desired end—and subsequently understands himself as the performer (*kartṛ*); thus, the agency of the qualified person (*adhikārin*) is also logically consistent.

Where a word denoting even a result, whether heard directly or supplied by implication, connects with the person and brings about a state of non-expectancy through that connection, there it is optional (*kāmyatā*).
Where non-expectancy arises through [the action] as qualified by another attribute, there it is obligatory (*nityatā*).
And the result, by the very force of its obligatoriness, is the avoidance of the loss of what is eternally desired.

And once a difference in the fruits [of the two rites] is established, there is a utility for the two sentences of entitlement (*adhikāra-vākya*) regarding the ritual characterized as the *darśapūrṇamāsa*.

Nor is there the defect of "heterogeneity" (*vairūpya*), whereby one of the two human qualifications—desire (*kāmanā*) and living (*jīvana*)—would have the fruit as its purpose while the other would have the occasion (*nimitta*) as its purpose; for such a distinction must necessarily be accepted because it is impossible for them both to be qualifications of the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*).

Furthermore, living cannot be a qualification of the person to be enjoined, because the entire duration of life is not something to be accomplished (*sādhya*), because simultaneity is impossible, and because mere living is not something that needs to be stated.
In the view that the word denotes the mere signifier (nimitta), however, the word "yāvat" is used to indicate repetition.
Therefore, it is established that there is no fault whatsoever in the position that [the word] denotes the means to the desired end (iṣṭasādhana).

Consequently, since there is no restrictive rule regarding the capacity of words to denote only that which is connected with an action to be accomplished (kāryānvita), he concludes that their capacity lies in being connected with something else (anyānvita)— Thus he summarizes: "Therefore, because there is no fixed rule for the semantic power of words to reside solely in what is connected with an action to be accomplished, their power resides in being connected with something else."
Therefore, the capacity of words to be connected with others is firmly established by the principles demonstrated according to their ability in the manner described above.
In this regard, it is well known that words bring about mutual connection through the power of expectancy, proximity, and semantic competency.
What is this expectancy? It is the desire to know, on the part of the cognizer, concerning another object once a word-meaning has been apprehended.
To the question "On what basis does it arise, or from what does it cease?", he says:
Because the denotation [of a word] does not reach its conclusion, and because there is a desire to know the meaning, it arises;
and because the purpose reaches its conclusion, that [desire] ceases with respect to the object of the word.

For one who maintains that words denote [meanings] as already connected (anvitābhidhāna), when a portion of the denotable meaning has been understood from the word due to the absence of other auxiliary factors, the denotation itself remains incomplete and generates a desire to know another portion of the denotable meaning.
In some cases, such as with the Viśvajit sacrifice and others, a desire for knowledge (*jijñāsā*) arises from the meaning itself.
And this twofold [desire] ceases once the connection with a purposeful object is established.
But what is "fitness" (*yogyatā*)? It is the capacity for syntactic connection (*anvaya-sāmarthya*) that brings about the cessation of the desire for knowledge.
What, then, is proximity (saṃnidhi)? It is the presence [of an object] in the mind without being interrupted by another word whose referent does not connect [with it].
Do words produce the cognition of a relation simultaneously through the power of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) and so forth, or rather successively? He says:
"And words extend the cognition of a relation only successively."
Because we observe that in linguistic usages there is a cognition of a sequential connection characterized by mutual expectancy:
when the word "cow" (gām) is uttered, the stem and the suffix, while making known the object-case-factor (karman) as excluded from non-cows, generate a desire to know the action.

However, through the proximity of the word "bring" (ānaya), these two—acting as its auxiliaries—then bring about the connection with the action. This is because we observe an expectancy for the meanings of words to be connected sequentially; thus, even for a word that has been used only once, it is logical that it can again serve as a cause for cognition when it is recalled upon the presence of its auxiliaries.

Therefore, it is established that words possess the capacity to convey relations because they have the power to denote meanings as already connected (*anvitābhidhāna*). Now, one might object: even if this were so, since the relationship between the denoter and the denoted is conventional (*sāṃketika*), and since speech—like that of the world—is of human origin (*pauruṣeya*), and since no other means of cognition is applicable regarding *dharma*, *adharma*, and *Brahman*, words lack authority (*prāmāṇya*) with respect to these matters. To this, he says:
"If the Veda is held to be produced by the unseen force (*apūrva*) and to function toward its own meaning..."
If it were a product, it would not be like the knowledge of God; [otherwise] there would be the fallacy of proving what is already established (siddhasādhana).

(65) If it is being proved that the Veda is "human" (pauruṣeya) in the sense of being produced by another means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) directed toward its own meaning, then there is a counter-inference (pratyanumāna): "The Veda is not produced by another means of valid cognition directed toward its own meaning, because—while lacking the nature of being the intellect or the effect of that [intellect] of a non-omniscient being—it is a means of valid cognition regarding dharma, adharma, and Brahman, just like the knowledge of God.
This is a counter-inference against both the proponents of God and those who maintain that the Veda is authoritative precisely because it is not human (apauruṣeya).
Now, if the Veda lacks authority regarding dharma and so forth, then the reason (hetu) is unestablished, and the example is devoid of its locus (āśraya-hīna), since there is no such thing as Īśvara.
What, then, is being proved?
If it is merely "being an effect" (kāryatāmātra), then it is a case of proving what is already established (siddhasādhana).
If phonemes are produced at each utterance, then those very same phonemes, when mounted upon a particular sequence, are denoted by the word "Veda"; thus, the Veda is produced at every utterance.
Alternatively, even if the phonemes are eternal, the Veda is nevertheless produced at every utterance as being conjoined with a specific sequence of perception and so forth.
Furthermore, because the succession of similarity in that specific sequence has no beginning in time, the Veda is designated as eternal.
Now, the novelty of the study of the Veda, as well as of the relationship between the designation and the designated, is being established.
Regarding this, he says:
"Just as the usage of the words 'study of the Veda' and their referents is [well-known] at present..."
In the same way, let inference proceed as follows:

[Thesis] The two practices of reciting the Veda and the usage of its words and meanings, which are the subjects of dispute, are based on such prior recitations and so forth; [Reason] because they are recitations of the Veda, etc.; [Example] like the present-day recitation of the Veda.

Nor can there be an inference of "being for the first time" (idamprathamatā) based on the fact that it is a recitation of a text, as in the case of the *Mahābhārata* and similar works; for an inference based on general observation (*sāmānyatodṛṣṭa*) is weaker when it contradicts an inference based on specific observation (*viśeṣatodṛṣṭa*), namely the fact that it is a recitation of the Veda.
Nor is there any contradiction with scripture, because the scriptural texts concerning creation have as their sole subject the mere fact of being produced.
[Objection: But surely the Lord, being omniscient according to scripture, will compose the Veda after perceiving dharma, adharma, and so forth.

[Reply: No, for omniscience is not established unless there is independent authority [for that knowledge]; moreover, the Lord is omniscient through his essential nature (svarūpa-jñāna), and in that state, unlike worldly beings, he lacks the instruments for composing sentences such as speech and the like, just as yogins lack them during the state of meditative absorption (yukta-avasthā).
Alternatively, one might construct a sentence by means of the speech and other faculties through the assumption of a body;
however, in that case, there would be no omniscience because consciousness is limited, just as in the case of yogis in their disembodied state.

Or, one might construct a sentence by perceiving everything through innate knowledge (*svarūpa-jñāna*), and then, having assumed a body, recollecting all that was perceived, one would produce the sentence.
This is not so, because there is an absence of residual impressions (*saṃskāra*) regarding the knowledge of intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*).
Nor is there any other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for dharma, adharma, and Brahman.
Regarding this, it has been said by those of our own school: "Let there be no fitness for another means of valid cognition in the case of dharma and adharma."

However, because Brahman is an existing entity (*bhūta*) and is thus capable of being apprehended by other means of knowledge, the Vedānta passages concerning it would necessarily be of human origin (*pauruṣeya*). Therefore, to avoid this [conclusion], it must be maintained that even those [Vedānta passages] are restricted to the domain of what is to be accomplished (*kāryaniṣṭha*).

Accordingly, in the rule *satsamprayoge*, the capacity [of Brahman] to be apprehended by other means of knowledge was rejected for the sake of establishing the non-human origin [of the Vedas]; for if such capacity existed, the Vedas would be of human origin.

This is not sound, because we observe that even sentences of the Buddha and others concerning unsuitable subjects are of human origin, while we also observe that even sentences concerning suitable subjects, such as "Vāyu is indeed the swiftest," are not of human origin.

Even when there is a connection with an injunction, it is not the injunction that is established by the explanatory passage (arthavāda), but rather praise and so forth, which are matters amenable to other means of knowledge.
Therefore, the cause for [the Veda] being non-human is something entirely different.
Now, let it be that it is not human-made; but from what [source] does its non-human origin derive?
Not so, because it is not impossible to establish.
How, then, is the authority of the Veda established? It is because, when it exists, it generates a cognition that is not sublated.
However, the sublation of verbal cognition occurs through the sublation of the cognition upon which it depends;
since it lacks human authorship, it has been stated that there is no dependence on another cognition.
Therefore, it is not sublated.
Therefore, it is established that verbal testimony is authoritative with respect to Brahman; thus he says:

"Therefore, words such as 'Real' (satya) and so forth, by virtue of their power to express a related meaning, inform us of an existing reality that is not the object of any other means of knowledge. (67)
Furthermore, which words convey the nature of Brahman, and which convey its conditioned form? To this, he says:
"By means of expressions for 'knowledge,' 'bliss,' and 'being' that function without conditions, the individual [Brahman] is conveyed through the denotation of its own universal. (68)

The words *jñāna* (knowledge), *ānanda* (bliss), and *sat* (being) denote both the higher and lower universals; because they share a common substratum (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), they indirectly indicate a single individual instance of bliss manifested by the lower universal through the medium of their own respective universals, characterizing it as Brahman.
This is seen from the co-occurrence of various higher and lower universals in a single locus, as in the expressions "the wall is a substance" or "the wall is being.
And thus: "From which indeed these beings are born..."
Having thus pointed out the definition (*lakṣaṇa*), [the text] points out the defined (*lakṣya*) Brahman-bliss with the words, "For indeed, from bliss alone these... and so forth.

In that context, the word "knowledge" (*jñāna*) is used to exclude [the notion] that bliss is illuminated by another, and the word "being" (*sat*) is used to exclude [the notion] that it is empty by its own nature.
Alternatively, since there is no bliss, knowledge, or being apart from Brahman, Brahman alone is denoted by words such as "being" and so forth due to its connection with those general properties.
[Objection: In that case, does it not follow that these terms are synonyms?
This is because [the term] functions through a distinction of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) that are opposed to emptiness, insentience, and suffering.
[Objection: But in that case, words such as "Being" (*sat*) and so forth would not have an unconditioned application (*nirupādhika-vṛtti*).
[Reply: This is not a fault.

Those [words] which produce a cognition regarding a single, determinate entity—whether with respect to a universal attribute (*sāmānyopādhi*) or an attribute opposed to suffering and so forth (*duḥkhādivirodhyupādhi*)—are "without attributes" (*nirupādhika*).
Words such as "not gross" (*asthūla*), however, have indeterminate entities as their objects and are dependent upon attributes (*upādhitantra*).
Now, one might object: even without establishing a state of opposition to what is non-existent (*tuccha*) and so forth, the conventional usage of terms like "existent" (*sat*) and so on is observed.
In that case, since even those things created by illusion (māyā) are perceived as being real bliss and consciousness, let the position of the universal (sāmānya) alone be adopted.
[Objection: But since even universals are of the nature of illusion, Brahman would not possess the form of bliss and so forth.

[Reply: No; because its nature as bliss and so forth consists merely in being the substratum of the universals of bliss and the rest, it does not depend upon being the substratum of ultimate (paramārtha) universals.
[Objection: Is it not the case that mother-of-pearl, when mixed with false silver, is not conventionally designated as "silver"?
[Reply: True; that is because it is an appearance of silver.
But here, since there is no other universal [to which they could correspond], those [universals] are merely appearances of universals.
Therefore, because it is the substratum of common attributes such as bliss and so forth, Brahman's nature as bliss and so forth is established.
Furthermore, the opposition to the falsity of that bliss is expressed by the word "Truth" (satya).
And the absence of delimitation by space, time, or substance is indicated by terms such as "non-dual," "infinite," and "Brahman."
By words such as "not gross" (asthūla) and so forth, the state of being free from phenomenal proliferation (niṣprapañcatā) is expressed;

by words such as "omniscient" (sarvajña) and so forth, the possession of attributes conditioned by phenomenal proliferation is described. Among these, the attributes conditioned by phenomenal proliferation are devoid of sublation as long as the phenomenal world exists, yet in their essential nature they consist of māyā.
Furthermore, since terms such as "not gross" (*asthūla*) and so forth consist in negation, they do not contradict the ultimate reality of non-duality.
Moreover, words such as "bliss" (*ānanda*) culminate in a single individual instance of bliss by means of an imagined universal;
because there is no presentation of a distinction between attribute and substrate, there is no contradiction with the ultimate reality of non-duality.
Alternatively, just like the word "space" (*ākāśa*), the word "existent" (*sat*) also denotes that single, independent Being which persists through jars and other objects;
meanwhile, the words "knowledge" (*jñāna*) and "bliss" (*ānanda*) will apply to it by way of their universals (*sāmānya*).

This being the case, there would be no need even for a "metaphor of the metaphorical" (*lakṣitalakṣaṇā*) based on the relationship between quality and the possessor of qualities (*guṇaguṇisambandha*).
Therefore, Brahman is established as one, without a second, and of the nature of bliss.
Likewise, he states that the identity of the individual soul (jīva) with Brahman is not characterized by superimposition (adhyāsa) and the like:
"The beginning and the conclusion, repetition, novelty, and the fruit [are the marks of the purport]."
And because of the corroborative arguments and the logical consistency, the individual soul (jīva) is therefore the Supreme.
In whatever sentence the sixfold marks of purport (tātparya-liṅga) are perceived with respect to a certain meaning, that sentence is determined to have that as its primary purport.
Thus, there is a uniformity between the introduction (upakrama) and the conclusion (upasaṃhāra).
The immortal has become mortal; the unknown has become known.
This whole world has that as its essence—it is one alone, without a second.
"Thou art That"—
thus also is there repeated practice.
Because of the repeated statement, "Thou art That— One only, without a second."
Likewise, there is also the quality of being previously unknown (*apūrvatā*);
for the identity of Brahman and the Self is not apprehended by any other means of knowledge whatsoever.
Similarly, there is also the result: "The man who has a teacher knows; for him, there is delay only so long [as he is not liberated]."
And so forth;
likewise, there is also an explanatory passage (arthavāda): "Having entered by means of this living self," and so on.
Likewise,

this same point is established by such passages as "Therefore they say of him, 'He sleeps,' for he has gone (apiita) into his own (svam)," which demonstrate that the body and senses are not the Self because they consist of food; and by the illustration of the heated axe, which explains liberation for one who has the firm conviction of the truth regarding the identity of the Self with Brahman as previously stated.
And in some places, by demonstrating non-attachment through the distinction from the three states [of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep].

Thus, since in the Vedānta texts the six marks of the purport of the sentences regarding the identity of the individual soul (*jīva*) with Brahman are understood as being either combined or optional according to the circumstances, this individual soul is indeed the Supreme Self; for, by its very nature, a word refers to its primary meaning and cannot be intended merely to convey a conceptual cognition.

Nor is there any contradiction with other means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*), because the conventional usage of difference is caused by the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of ignorance (*avidyā*). Thus he says:
Ignorance (avidyā) is a limiting adjunct (upādhi) that causes differentiation; it is neither a separate entity nor a cognition (dhī).
This is because [ignorance] depends on duality, because it would be equivalent [to the self], and because it is not observed in states such as deep sleep.

"You do not know Him who generated these [beings]; another has surely come between you. Enveloped by mist, prattling and satisfied with the breath of life, the reciters of hymns (ukthaśāsaḥ) wander about. (Ṛgveda 10.82.7)
In this mantra, after stating,
"Thus there arose another interval between you," when the inquiry arises as to what that interval was:
From the phrase "enveloped by mist," it is understood that mist acts as an obscuring agent;
and this darkness is not external, but rather internal.
And that [reality] is distinct from both being and non-being, according to such scriptural passages as: "There was neither being nor non-being; there was only darkness."
Abiding within the self, I destroy the darkness born of ignorance with the radiant lamp of knowledge.
And because of the traditional teaching (smṛti) that it is removable by knowledge,
it is therefore nothing other than ignorance (ajñāna).
"When ignorance, which produces the sense of duality, has gone to absolute destruction..."
Who could create a non-existent difference between the Self and Brahman?
Thus, the Smṛti shows that ignorance alone is the veiling factor.
Now, when the inquiry arises as to whose ignorance it is and in what it resides, it must be stated that it belongs to the individual soul (jīva) with respect to Brahman.
Consequently, in the absence of ignorance, one would have to postulate some other distinction to account for the division between the individual soul and Brahman.

Therefore, even if there were such a surplus, since the requirement for duality remains the same—namely, "whose" and "from what"—if that which is characterized by the surplus were the individual soul (*jīva*), and if that [soul] were removable through knowledge, it would not differ from the position that [the soul] is ignorance (*ajñāna*). If, on the other hand, the qualified [entity] were the individual soul, there would be no liberation.
Thus, this [argument] is trivial.
Nor is mere cognition (*dhī*) alone the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of the individual soul, because the individual soul is perceived even in deep sleep, when that [cognition] is not perceived.
Therefore, ignorance alone is the cause of differentiation;
and that ignorance is removed in its entirety only through immediate knowledge (*aparokṣajñāna*). And that immediate knowledge arises from the Word (*śabda*) alone—thus he says:
Because it arises from the object, because of the identity of consciousness with the object, or because of the removal of ignorance;

since [knowledge] is not established by itself, immediate perception (*aparokṣya*) arises from the Word. (71) In the world as well, immediate perception occurs either because consciousness arises from the object, or because the object is identical with consciousness, or because the object—which, having the nature of consciousness, is itself non-different from the conscious self—has its veil destroyed. Knowledge caused by that is called "immediate knowledge" (*aparokṣajñāna*), neither merely because of an inherent immediacy in the knowledge itself, nor because of the consciousness produced by it.

In the same way, regarding Brahman as well, the cognition that is the cause of verbal knowledge is of the nature of Brahman and non-different from Brahman—either because all consciousnesses have Brahman as their material cause (*prakṛti*), or because it is immediate (*aparokṣa*) due to the destruction of the veil over the self-luminous [Brahman], or because it is a cognition of the Self like the "I"-cognition (*ahaṃpratyaya*).
The knowledge caused by that is called immediate knowledge (*aparokṣajñāna*).

Even when such knowledge has arisen from words, it may appear as if indirect (*parokṣa*) due to defects such as incredulity (*asambhāvanā*), or through error, owing to the force of the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of ignorance (*avidyā*).

And because that [mind] is purified through reflection (*manana*), meditative absorption (*nididhyāsana*), and so forth, it becomes capable of perceiving subtle objects; thus, when the referent of the term "thou" (*tvaṃpadārtha*)—which is distinct from the body and the senses—is manifested through direct perception, the mind transforms into the form of the knowledge of Brahman as the Self. Through this stabilization, even though the fire lasts for only two moments and does not burn in a single moment, it nevertheless burns [the fuel] in those two moments.
Therefore, he states that this is established:
"Hence, the determination of the verbal [scripture] is for the sake of attaining the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*)."
This [work], which is connected with a distinguished fruit, should be heard by one who desires to know it.
(72) Those who have known everything that is to be known do not praise even that which has been composed by great men in this world; how much less so that which is by someone like me?
Thus, though engaged in this fruitless expenditure of words for the sake of purifying my own intellect, may the virtuous forgive me.
I bow to him who, through the manifestation of his own nature as Brahman, awakened by himself, [attained liberation].
Even in its meaning, this is not merely a matter of names; it is the Guru who has no other experience [than this].
Having prostrated before Janārdana, the venerable Yatīndra has composed this *Śabdanirṇaya* for the enlightenment of the ignorant. (74–75)
